title: Integrity Turnitin – Canvas Plagiarism Framework for Instructors
body:
The Canvas Plagiarism Framework (CPF) is an easy-to-use method of obtaining Turnitin Similarity & Originality Reports for submitted assignments in Canvas. Turnitin features are configured via Canvas assignment settings and accessible from within Feedback Studio. In addition to its ease of use, the Canvas Plagiarism Framework offers several advantages over the Turnitin External Tool integration.
•	All access and due date settings are pulled directly from the Canvas assignment settings. This avoids the common Turnitin errors that occur when importing assignments from past courses.
•	Supports Group Assignments.
•	Supports Canvas Peer Review assignments.
•	Multiple submissions are supported, with each submission receiving its own Similarity Report.
•	Re-submissions are permitted after the Due Date.
For more information on the Canvas Plagiarism Framework’s features, check out the full product comparison chart.
To Enable Canvas Plagiarism Framework (Turnitin)
1.	Create a new assignment or go to an existing assignment you wish to enable Turnitin for.
2.	In the assignment settings, select Online as the assignment Submission Type.

     Error! Filename not specified.
3.	Under Online entry options, select the File Uploads and/or Text entry checkbox.
4.	Select Turnitin from the Plagiarism Review drop-down menu.

     Error! Filename not specified.
5.	Customize the Turnitin Plagiarism settings as desired. To learn more about configuring the platform, check out the Turnitin settings documentation.
6.	Make any adjustments to the remaining Canvas assignment settings as desired, including making this a group assignment, requiring Peer Reviews, and setting the access and due dates.
7.	Click Save when done or Save & Publish to make the assignment available to students.
As Canvas may not immediately notify Turnitin that an assignment has been created, we advise waiting 90 seconds between creating the assignment and making the first submission. This will allow Canvas to notify Turnitin that the assignment has been created.
The Similarity Report
Instructors can access the Similarity Reports in either SpeedGrader or Gradebook by clicking the colored icon as indicated in either:

If the Show originality report to students option has been enabled, students can view their Originality Report when it is made available by clicking the icon in Gradebook.

title: Integrity Turnitin – Recommended Syllabus Statement
body:
In coordination with the Office of General Counsel, Rutgers Office of Information Technology advises instructors who use Turnitin for plagiarism detection to include the following statement in their course syllabus:
 
Students agree that, by taking this course, all required papers may be submitted to Turnitin.com (directly or via the learning management system) for textual similarity review and plagiarism detection. All submitted papers will be included as source documents in the Turnitin.com reference database solely for the purpose of detecting plagiarism of such papers. Use of the Turnitin.com service is subject to the Usage Policy posted on the Turnitin.com site.
 
Students who disagree should contact the course instructor immediately.
 
For students who elect not to submit directly to Turnitin, instructors may accept digital copies of the assignment and submit them on the student's behalf via the Turnitin website.
If you have any questions, please contact your LMS Help Desk.

title: General Support Course Accessibility - Audio/Video (Live Content)
body:
Auto Captions available
Bronze Level
Most platforms will allow users to enable closed captioning. Below are some tools for auto-captioning videos and conversations in real time. It's important to note these tools are not designed for post-processing editing. It's also important to note that auto-captions are about 80% accurate.
•	How to enable Zoom Auto-captions
•	How to enable WebEx Auto-Captions
•	How to enable MS Teams Auto-Captions
•	Zip Captions | Online - Free
This tool allows you to generate captions from any audio your computer receives. It allows you to stream those captions to audience members.
•	Google Live Caption | Google Chrome - Free
Built into Google Chrome and Chrome Books, you can have any video automatically display captions. See Google's instructions on how to turn on live caption.
•	Live Transcribe | Android - Free
Built into all Android devices, you can instantly get captions on any video or audio from the microphone. This is a great way of getting instant auto-captions for real-time conversations
•	iOS Live Captions | iPhones/iOS devices - Free
With this, you can get real-time auto-captioning of spoken text, as well as any video displayed on your phone.
•	MacOS Live Captions | MacOS devices- Free
It provides real-time auto-captions for any audio in any app, including Facetime, Zoom, or videos played in your browser.
•	Windows Live Captions | Windows - Free
Provides real-time auto-captioning for any video played on your Windows device.
•	Otter Ai | Free- with paid upgrades
Provides a real-time transcript while recording the audio. It allows you to go back and review the transcript. Otter provides speaker identification, post-recording outlines/summaries, and an ability to collaborate with others.
Instructor created videos
Silver Level
It's important to remember that individuals who are blind will not be able to see the content shown on your screen. Thus, vocalizing anything you show is important, whether images or written text.
Other important considerations:
•	Avoid using words like "this" or "that", which refer to what is visually being shown without detail.
•	When demonstrating how to perform functions, avoid saying things like "click here". Instead, describe what you are doing, i.e. "click on the home button", "click on the icon that says 'remove duplicates'", etc.
•	Avoid referring to things by color, i.e. "the green bar".
•	Providing PowerPoints and other presented materials beforehand allows the student to review them before class.
Professional Caption/ASL interpreter
All items should have a professional Caption/ASL interpreter available.
Gold Level
If you have a student with a disability in your class who is approved for captioning, Rutgers Access and Disability Resources (RADR) should have contacted you. If a student has made themselves known to you, and you have not heard from RADR, have that student reach out to their coordinator to ensure they submit all of the appropriate requests.
It's important to note that in some cases, the captions may be viewed by the student through a third-party site and not directly through your video conferencing tool. If you do not see the professional captions appear, this may be the reason.

title: General Support Course Accessibility - Audio/Video (Prerecorded)
body:
All video content is in Kaltura
Bronze Level
We recommend that all your Video Content within Canvas be uploaded to Kaltura first. This provides several benefits:
•	It creates automated captions for students who may need captioning
•	It allows disability services to request professional captioning on that video, should there be a student with a disability in your class, without you needing to do any additional work
Learn more about Kaltura and how to upload videos.
Once uploaded to Kaltura, we recommend you embed those videos directly into Canvas. Any changes to those videos, such as adding professional captions, will automatically be reflected in the videos in Canvas.
Auto-captions are available with the ability to turn on/off
Bronze Level
It's important to note that auto-captions are about 70-80% accurate and may not meet the needs of students with disabilities. Automated captions are a minimum requirement for all Rutgers courses. The best practice however (the Gold Standard) is to have professional captioning, or instructor reviewed and edited captioning on all videos.
If you are utilizing a third-party video that you cannot download and utilize Kaltura with, you must check that the video has auto-captions available. The video player should allow the user to turn on and off those captions at a minimum. On some platforms like YouTube, you can filter your search results by those videos with captions.
If you are utilizing a YouTube video, Kaltura has the ability to upload that YouTube video to Kaltura. It is better to upload those items to Kaltura rather than copy and paste a YouTube link into your course.
Instructor-created videos have all items described
Silver Level
In many cases, you may create content by voicing over PowerPoints or using a service like WeVideo to create recorded lecture material. It's important to remember that individuals who are blind will not be able to see the content shown on their screen in a video format. Thus, it's important to vocalize anything you show, whether images or written text.
Other important considerations:
•	Avoid using words like "this" or "that", that refer to what is visually being shown without detail.
•	When demonstrating how to perform functions, avoid saying things like "click here". Instead, describe what you are doing, i.e, click on the home button, click on the icon that says 'remove duplicates', etc.
•	Avoid referring to things by color, i.e., "the green bar".
All items should have professional captioning done
Gold Level
If you have a student with a disability in your class who is approved for captioning, Rutgers Access and Disability Resources (RADR) should have contacted you. If a student has made themselves known to you, and you have not heard from RADR, have that student reach out to their coordinator to ensure they submit all of the appropriate requests.
It's important to note that videos can take up to 2 weeks to caption. Having your videos in Kaltura, along with a list of any third-party video sources you might be using, will help RADR submit those items to be captioned.
Items should have extended audio descriptions available
Gold Level
If you have a student who is blind in your course, videos may require audio descriptions. This can take 3-4 weeks and sometimes longer, depending on the length of the video. Having your videos in Kaltura, along with a list of any third-party video sources you might be using, will help RADR submit those items to be audio-described.

title: General Support Course Accessibility - Document Accessibility
body:
Meaningful heading structure
Bronze Level
Heading structures with a distinct visual style help individuals with visual impairments understand how a document is organized. Appropriate headings are secondary navigation tools that help readers skim and scan the document.
Headings should fit an outline. Making text larger or bolder does not make it a heading in Word.
To Add headings to a document
Use the built-in heading styles to apply uniform heading structure to Word documents.
Word Styles contain preconfigured headings understood by assistive technology (e.g., Heading 1- Heading 6). These headings are available under the Styles section in the Home tab of the Ribbon.
Apply the “Heading 1” style for the main heading and “Heading 2” for sub-headings. Additional organization and division of topics should use the appropriate head style: “Heading 3,” “Heading 4,” etc., without going past "Heading 6." 
Error! Filename not specified.
Use the Home tab’s Styles menu to add heading styles.
Verify headings
Every heading in a document can be verified using the Navigation Pane, located in the Show group on the View tab of the Ribbon.
This pane also allows users to navigate to any section of the document by clicking on the corresponding heading. 
Error! Filename not specified.
Use the View tab to add navigation panes.
No use of color or shape to identify meaning
Bronze Level
Do not use color or shapes to identify meaning, as someone with color blindness or someone with low vision might be unable to distinguish between the two options. For example, rather than using a green dot 🟢 to signify something is Open, you can write "Open."
Meaningful/Descriptive Links
Bronze Level
Hyperlink text must be clear and meaningful, with enough contextual information that a user would understand the link’s destination.
You shouldn’t use “click here,” “read more,” and “learn more” as the only words linked.
•	Do: “Read our strategic plan.”
•	Don't: “Click here for our strategic plan.”
Similarly, don’t use the same link language for two different destinations. For example, if “Contact Us” is listed as a link twice on the same page, it should take users to the same place.
Accessible Tables
Bronze Level
Microsoft products can only produce simple tables, which only have 1 heading row and 1 heading column at max. There are several steps to creating an accessible table:
1.	Should this be a table?
If your table should actually be a list, it is better to make that a bulleted list rather than using a table format. Additionally, if you are using a table for styling purposes, like creating 2 columns of text, it's better to use the Microsoft 'Column' option to create those columns.
2.	Do I need to simplify the table?
If you have a complex table, with nested content, and multiple heading rows or columns, you will need to break those tables into smaller ones to allow the screen reader to read it correctly.
3.	Designate a heading row.
The "Table Style Options" section of the ribbon on the Table Tools contextual tab lets you indicate that your data has a header row. 
Error! Filename not specified.
4.	Repeat Column headings
Column headings should be repeated at the top of a table if the table spans multiple pages.
To repeat the column headings: 
o	Right-click the table, and then select Table Properties.
o	In the "Table Properties" dialog box, select the Row tab.
o	In the "Options" group, ensure the "Repeat as header" row at the top of each page is checked.
o	Uncheck the box next to Allow row to break across pages.
o	Select OK to accept the changes.
5.	Add alternative text to the table.
To add alternative text for tables, use the Alt Text tab of the "Table Properties" dialog box. You can do this by right-clicking on the table, selecting Table Properties, and then selecting the Alt-Text tab.  
Error! Filename not specified.
Use of PowerPoint (PPT) template layouts only
Bronze Level
PowerPoint has several built-in layouts: A title slide, a Title with one content section, a Title with two content areas, etc.
Error! Filename not specified.
Using these layouts will ensure that your PowerPoints have the correct reading order and titles for every slide and that there are no floating objects that might be difficult for a screen reader to access.
If you are unsure of how to make accessible PowerPoints, avoid adding floating textboxes or floating images (items not part of the standard layout). Additionally, avoid using the blank slide unless it is truly a blank slide.
Clean copies of printed/scanned materials
Provide clean copies of printed/scanned materials. This includes handouts, course reserves, course packs, etc.
Bronze Level
Avoid using content that is smudged, have words cut off, or is difficult for you to read. If you have a hard time reading it, someone with low vision or who is blind will be unable to read it.
Searchable PDFs only
Bronze Level
Searchable PDFs are those in which the text is rendered as actual text and not images. A simple way of knowing if this is the case is by seeing if you can highlight the text. If you cannot, Adobe Acrobat has an OCR function that allows you to digitize that PDF into a searchable PDF. Additionally, you can use tools like Sensus Access to convert your document.
Color contrast 
Silver Level
For any content you create, you must run the Accessibility Checker in Word.
One of the things it will identify is color contrast issues in the text you wrote. It will also suggest font color changes to help meet guidelines.
Error! Filename not specified.
Alternative formats available
Gold Level
If you have a student who is blind in your class or a student who needs an alternative format for their course materials, you should speak with the student's coordinator to better understand those needs.
In some cases, as with those students who are blind, Rutgers Access and Disability Resources will reach out to you ahead of time to collect your course content and assist with making those items accessible. There are a few things that can significantly help ensure students have access to your content at the same time as the class:
•	Have your syllabus complete before the start of the semester, and include any required readings, including textbook information.
•	Have your content ready at least 2 weeks before the class you intend on showing it.
•	Alt-text any images you have in any of the documents you use. You are the content expert, and knowing what those images represent is difficult for whoever may remediate your document.
High-contrast text
Use high-contrast text (e.g., black text on a white background). Use an 11-point or larger font size.
Gold Level
If you have a student with low vision, you may see that they are approved for enlarged font. The Letter of Accommodation will typically indicate the font size (i.e., 14pt font). For any course documents you create, whether that be PowerPoint or Word handouts (like review sheets), you should consider:
•	Make sure to use high-contrast foreground and background colors. These color combinations include White and Black (i.e., black text on a white background or white text on a black background), Black and Yellow, and Blue and Yellow.
•	Ensuring your font size is minimally the size indicated on the Letter of Accommodation. If none is listed, using 14pt font should be your standard. If the font size becomes too big for a PowerPoint, consider making a Word document with the equivalent information as the PPT the student can follow.

title: General Support Course Accessibility - Images
body:
Instructor created content
All instructor-created content must have a useful alt text for all images.
Bronze Level
Alternative text for images, also known as alt text, describes an image read by assistive technology. It also helps search engines understand the content of an image, which can improve SEO ( search engine optimization).
The alt text should convey the purpose and function of the non-text content. This means the same image may have different alt text depending on its context and purpose. For example, an image used for marketing will have different alt text than the same image used for training purposes.
Alt text is more of an art than a science. The only "wrong" is not including alt text where needed. Considering alt text on a scale of "good" versus "better," will you help craft more useful alt text.
How to add an alternative text to:
•	A Microsoft Word or PowerPoint file
•	A Google Document or Presentation
General Guidelines
•	Keep the alt text concise (no more than 10-15 words).
•	If the image contains words, include the words in the alt text.
•	If the image is used as a link or control, the alt text should help form the link text or control label.
•	If the alt text would be redundant to neighboring text, treat the image as if it is decorative.
Training Workshop
For general information on accessibility training, please visit the Rutgers Digital Accessibility website.
Student created content
Students are provided with instructions/expectations on how to add alt text to the content they create.
Silver Level
Faculty may often use third-party software that allows students to create content in discussion forums, messages, etc. It's important that you provide students with directions on how to make their content accessible.

title: General Support Course Accessibility - Managing PDFs
body:
With all of your PDFs, you should follow our PDF workflow: 
1.	Remove any unused PDFs from your course. TidyUp is an excellent tool for doing this.
2.	Reorganize your site. For those documents that you'd like to keep but are for archival purposes only, you should move them to a folder clearly marked "Archived."
3.	Reformat your PDF. If your document was originally a Word or PowerPoint file, we recommend uploading that version instead of the PDF. You can upload read-only files to ensure the content remains the same. We recommend converting PDFs that could be webforms or module pages to webforms/html pages.
4.	Remediate the remainder. For those PDFs that genuinely need to be PDFs, we recommend you utilize tools like SensusAccess to provide text-based documents to your students.

title: General Support Course Accessibility - Reviewing Current Courses
body:
We recommend following the steps outlined below to help you improve the accessibility of your courses:
1.	Run CidiLabs Tidy Up. 
o	TidyUp scans the Canvas course for unused pages and unlinked files and removes them from the course.
o	Access TidyUp through Rutgers Canvas by enabling it in the course navigation.
2.	Review course content through Ally Course Accessibility Report.
o	Ally will help you gain detailed insight into the accessibility of your course content, provide guidance on how to remediate inaccessible components of your content, and provide students with a range of alternative formats.
o	You can access the Course Accessibility Report through the course navigation menu on the left side of your course. If you do not see the Accessibility Report available, you can enable it via your course navigation settings.
3.	Determine your priorities.
If you have already developed materials for your course, we recommend choosing one of the options below as a starting point: 
o	Start with your syllabus 
	Making your syllabus accessible is a great place to start on making your course more accessible as it is one of the first documents your students will be accessing and will get you familiar with the document remediation process.
	Tools such as Microsoft Word and PowerPoint have accessibility checkers in their software that point out which sections of your document need remediation. Some common accessibility issues include incorrect text headers, color contrast issues, and missing alt text on images. 
	Rutgers IT Document Accessibility Guide
	Improving Microsoft Documents with Accessibility Checker
o	Use the Web Content Helper to help prioritize based on your course’s unique context. 
	This tool will help you prioritize the remediation changes that will have the most impact on students in your class. Depending on how you respond to the questions, the Web Content Helper will identify which level of consideration should be taken for your course.
	The base-level for all courses is our Bronze Model, with increasing levels of accessibility/usability thresholds according to factors like class size and enrollment of students with disabilities.
	The goal is to provide you with a road map of the items that are going to make the most impact in your course as you work overtime to improve the accessibility of your course.
o	Use the Ally Course Report to see your course’s accessibility score and set a manageable goal, such as raising your overall score by 10%. 
	The Ally Course Accessibility Report can help you determine a pathway to a more accessible course that works for you. The report separates content into two groups, “content with the easiest issues to fix” and “low scoring content.” 
	Remediating content with the easiest issues to fix is a good way to quickly fix issues such as missing alt text on images.
	Going after the lowest-scoring content will have the most impact on raising your course’s overall accessibility score.
	It’s a good idea to set a goal of raising your overall course accessibility by 10% per semester. The most important thing is to begin working accessibility into your course design process in a consistent, ongoing way.
Other considerations
As you remediate your course files, here are other things you should consider.
Resource Selection
Some scanned documents can be too difficult to read. Scanned documents with text cut off, smudges, faded writing, etc., may not be feasible to make into an accessible document. You should review your course resources to make sure that the resources provided are legible.
Use the Rutgers Library Academic Search Premier to find updated and legible resources. Work with your content area librarian to locate accessible versions of any other resources you may need.
Review Course Technologies
When utilizing course technologies, prioritize using native Canvas features like Canvas Discussions, Quizzes, and Modules, as they are accessible to students. While third-party external tools may offer additional features, they can create inaccessible experiences for some students, although some tools have or are being updated to include accessibility options.
PDFs
With all of your PDFs, you should follow our PDF workflow:
1.	Remove any unused PDFS from your course. TidyUp is an excellent tool for doing this.
2.	If you would like to keep your unused PDF documents for archival purposes, please move them to a separate sandbox course clearly marked Archived.
3.	If your document was originally a Word or PPT file, upload the original version of the document instead of the PDF. You can upload read-only files to ensure the content remains the same. If possible, please convert PDF files to module pages. It is easier for students who are using screen readers to navigate pages than it is for students who are using attached files.
4.	For those PDFs that genuinely need to be PDFs, we recommend you utilize SensusAccess to provide text-based documents to your students.

title: General Support Minimum Course Accessibility Guidelines
body:
We've developed a list of items to help you create more accessible courses. It's important to note that document and digital accessibility is only a small piece of making your course accessible. We recommend you read the following pages to help walk you through other important information you should know:
•	Accessible Design Guide - This guide will inform you about important design choices when making content that will significantly benefit your students. It will also give you essential information about how to structure/conduct your lectures.
•	Hosting Accessible Trainings - While this was written with workshops in mind, this will give you great insight into best teaching practices.
Overview of the standards
To make accessibility more achievable and reflect the students in your class being able to benefit the most, we've developed a good, better, best model.
Bronze Level
In this model, the Bronze level is the minimum level of accessibility that we would like all courses to reach. It is based on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) version 2.1 Level A. This is the minimum level countries/organizations could choose to adopt. Here in the U.S., the DOJ has adopted Level AA, and thus, courses in this category do not meet the full letter of the law for course accessibility.
This level is meant to provide you with an achievable first step and allow an easy pathway to Silver (based mostly on WCAG 2.1 AA). Bronze is a baseline for courses and is not intended to be your final outcome.
Silver Level
For courses above a certain enrollment, we ask all those courses to achieve a Silver level. This was based on WCAG 2.1 AA but also considers that certain aspects of WCAG may be more difficult for faculty to achieve without help/intervention from others on campus, i.e., the Office of Disability Services (ODS).
The items in this category are meant to be easily achievable given the foundation you have laid from the bronze level, and it also sets up departments like ODS and Rutgers Access and Disability Services to easily provide accommodations/support for students needing accommodations.
Gold Level
Any course with a student with a disability approved for accommodations falls into this level. This level fully conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA and details offices you should work with to achieve certain accommodations (like ASL Interpreters).
Considerations on how to use these levels
Ideally, this should be a gradient of colors instead of three distinct colors side by side. We've created a form that allows you to determine your minimum base level and then adds only those specific guidelines that apply to your course. For example, if you have a student with a disability, and that student is approved for an ASL interpreter, we can make general assumptions about the nature of their disability. Knowing this, we will provide you with Silver level as your base level, and for all those that apply to this student, we'll provide you with Gold level items. To put it into practice, you'll see items about professional video captioning (another accommodation they have) but not audio descriptions, as this student is likely a sighted student and doesn't require audio descriptions.
The goal is to provide you a road map of the items that are going to make the most impact in your course as you work overtime to improve the accessibility of your course.

title: Discontinuation of Adobe Creative Cloud Synced files
body:
On October 1, 2024, Adobe discontinued the Creative Cloud Files sync service. Rutgers did not decide this change. This service enables people to save files on their local devices in a folder called Creative Cloud Files. The contents of this folder could be synced (copied) to your cloud storage on Creative Cloud. These files can be accessed locally on your device through the folder named Creative Cloud Files or through the Creative Cloud website under Synced files located within the Launch More menu.
What happened?
After Synced files were discontinued, Creative Cloud file syncing was no longer supported as an option. Adobe also removed the Synced files section on the Creative Cloud website and permanently deleted the assets within the cloud storage folder Synced files. 
Additional information
All assets in your Creative Cloud Files folder will remain intact on your local device and will not be deleted from there. However, sharing links to these files will no longer work. You may choose to leave the assets in the Creative Cloud Files folder, or you can choose to move them to other cloud storage options. 
Adobe continues to offer and support cloud storage and syncing across Creative Cloud with Cloud Documents and Creative Cloud Libraries. This change impacts none of these cloud storage solutions.
Your local devices' Creative Cloud Files folder will be visible and retain any files you have previously synced. You can then rename the folder as you see fit.
For additional assistance, please contact the OIT Help Desk.

title: Creative Cloud Adobe account audits
body:
Who can have an Adobe Creative Cloud account?
According to the Office of Information Technology guidelines, only the following classes of people are eligible to have Adobe accounts:
•	Current employees of Rutgers University
•	Current students
•	Professor Emeritus
•	Guests: individuals who are conducting University business and are directly associated with the University, but are not officially on the University's payroll. For example, visiting professors/scholars, members of auxiliary groups, and others who are working on University business or affiliated with the University.
The following groups of people are not automatically eligible to Adobe accounts:
•	Former employees (including teaching/graduate assistants who may still be students but are not actively working for Rutgers)
•	Employees of other organizations who are performing work at Rutgers
•	Alumni
•	Retirees
Any of the above may be eligible for a guest account if a department or division of Rutgers is willing to sponsor them. Please see the Guest Account page for further information.
Recently hired employees who have not yet been added to the payroll system and therefore have not been assigned a Faculty or Staff role may have their department's payroll person use the Early Employee NetID form to request an early role.
How can I keep my Adobe account?
We determine which accounts should be closed by comparing Adobe accounts with the active roles (e.g., Faculty, Staff) of usernames listed in the University's Open Registry (OR) service, which serves as the basis for the Rutgers Online Directory. The OR may have some information that requires correction.
Current Employees
You may not be listed in the OR as a current employee. To check this, go to the Search for People tool and search for your name. Review each result if you get more than one. If your name does not appear, contact your department's Human Resources person.
When your entry appears, review the information there. If it is incorrect, contact your department's Human Resources person.
After your department’s Human Resources person has corrected your record, your department’s Rutgers Delegated Administrator can verify that your account is no longer subject to closure.
Students
You may not be listed in the OR as a current student. To check this, go to the Search for People tool and search for your name. Review each result if you get more than one. If your name does not appear, inquire about your registration via One Stop.
When your entry appears, review the information there. If it is incorrect, please inquire about your registration via One Stop.
Guests
If you are affiliated with Rutgers but not employed full-time by the university, you may request a guest account. Have a sponsor from the department you are working with visit the Guest Account site and submit a request on your behalf, which will be sent to our Accounts Office for processing.
Every year, you must renew your guest account. You will be notified when the time to renew your account arrives (30 days prior to the expiration of the account).
Your Rutgers Connect Delegated Administrator can assist your sponsor with submitting a Guest Account request and creating your Adobe account, if necessary.
Others
If you do not fit into any of the above categories, you may want to try contacting a department at Rutgers related to your work and ask if they would be willing to sponsor a Guest account for you.
We have no mechanism in place for individuals who are no longer associated with Rutgers to pay a fee and thus retain their accounts. These individuals should be able to pay for a full account on their own and transfer their data before losing access to their account.
What is the typical account audit timeline?
Once an account is found to be ineligible for Adobe:
•	On day one, i.e., the same day, it is found to be ineligible: The account is sent an email notification.
•	On day seven, i.e., approximately one week later: The account is locked out of Adobe.
•	On day thirty-five, i.e., approximately 5 weeks later: The account is deleted from Adobe.
Note: If the account is found to be eligible for Adobe at any time before deletion, it will be removed from the audit.
What should I do before the account is closed?
If you are about to lose your Adobe account, you may want to take the following steps.
•	Contact the IT staff in your department to determine the correct protocol for the data (files) in your account.
•	You will lose access to your Adobe files once your account is deleted, so it's recommended that you save them to an alternative location. Adobe has instructions on how to manually transfer your data, which must be done before losing access to your Rutgers Adobe account. Contact your local IT staff to assist with this process.
What happens after the account is closed?
After your account is closed, you will lose access to your Adobe account.
Approximately 4 weeks after your account is closed, your Adobe account will be deleted.
When an account is deleted, you will no longer be able to access Adobe services
For further assistance
If you have questions about any of the above, you can send an email to help@oit.rutgers.edu or contact the OIT Help Desk.

title: Platform and API Services
body:
Getting Started with ChatGPT Chat, Codex and Work at Rutgers" "
The ChatGPT desktop app is an AI-powered tool developed by OpenAI that includes three modules: ChatGPT Codex (an AI coding agent that can read, edit, and run code directly on your machine), ChatGPT Chat (conversational AI), and ChatGPT Work (workflow automation). The app is available for macOS and Windows, with a terminal CLI, IDE extensions for VS Code and other editors, and a cloud based interface also available. ChatGPT Codex can handle a wide range of software engineering tasks, including writing new features, fixing bugs, refactoring code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.
The ChatGPT desktop app requires either an active ChatGPT subscription or an API key configured through Portkey. Rutgers faculty, staff, and students can purchase a ChatGPT Edu subscription through the University Software Portal, which provides enterprise-grade data protections and ensures your data is not used to train OpenAI’s models. Alternatively, some ChatGPT Codex and ChatGPT Cowork features can be accessed by configuring a custom API provider such as Rutgers’ Portkey gateway, which routes requests through the university’s enterprise AI infrastructure.
Table of Contents
•	Appropriate Use 
o	ChatGPT Work
o	ChatGPT Codex
o	General Conversations
•	Safety and Data Protection 
o	Use Your Rutgers ChatGPT Account
o	What You Should Know
o	Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
•	Understanding Costs: ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are Agentic Systems, Not a Chatbot 
o	Usage and Rate Cards
o	What ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex Are Designed For
o	What ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are NOT Designed For
•	How to Get Started 
o	Option 1: Purchase a ChatGPT Edu Subscription and Download the ChatGPT Desktop App (Recommended)
o	Option 2: Sign In with a Rutgers ChatGPT Edu Subscription (CLI)
o	Option 3: Use Portkey API Integration
•	Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Other Access Methods
•	Other Free AI Tools at Rutgers
•	Links
Appropriate Use
ChatGPT Work
ChatGPT Work is an agentic workspace for complex knowledge work. ChatGPT Work can autonomously work through multi-step tasks and interact with files on your computer. At this time, Rutgers OIT is not approving integrations between ChatGPT and third-party applications. This is due to ongoing evaluation of security requirements and the need to establish formal policies and governance. Use it for:
•	Document analysis - Upload files and documents for ChatGPT Work to analyze, summarize, cross-reference, and discuss.
•	Research and synthesis - Explore topics, synthesize information from multiple sources, and organize findings.
•	Project planning - Break down complex tasks, outline approaches, and work through problems step by step.
•	Writing and editing - Draft, revise, and refine documents with ChatGPT Work, autonomously revising through multiple rounds.
•	Data processing - ChatGPT Work can run code in an isolated environment to process data, generate visualizations, and produce reports.
As with all AI tools, always review AI-generated content for accuracy before using it in any official capacity.
ChatGPT Codex
ChatGPT Codex is a powerful tool for accelerating software development workflows in academic and professional settings. Common use cases include:
•	Writing code - Generate new functions, classes, modules, or entire project scaffolds from natural language descriptions.
•	Debugging - Identify and fix bugs by describing the problem or pointing ChatGPT Codex at failing tests.
•	Refactoring - Restructure existing code for clarity, performance, or maintainability.
•	Code review - Get an AI-assisted review of changes before committing or submitting pull requests.
•	Running tests - Let ChatGPT Codex execute your test suite and iterate on fixes until tests pass.
•	Learning and exploration - Ask ChatGPT Codex to explain unfamiliar code, libraries, or programming concepts.
•	Automation - Script repeatable workflows using the codex exec command for batch operations.
Always review AI-generated code for correctness, security vulnerabilities, and adherence to your project’s standards before committing it. ChatGPT Codex can produce plausible but incorrect code, introduce subtle bugs, or use outdated patterns.
General Conversations
For simple questions and quick tasks that don’t require agentic capabilities, consider using the Chat tab instead of the Work tab in the ChatGPT desktop app as well as Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini - they are far more cost-effective for conversational and single-turn tasks.
Safety and Data Protection
Use Your Rutgers ChatGPT Account
When you sign in to the ChatGPT desktop app with a Rutgers ChatGPT Edu account, your data is protected by OpenAI’s enterprise-level data handling agreements with the university. Your conversations, code, and data are not used to train OpenAI’s models. This protection does not apply when using a personal ChatGPT account.
If you are using the ChatGPT desktop app through the Portkey API integration instead of a ChatGPT login, your requests are routed through Rutgers’ enterprise Portkey instance and are similarly protected under the university’s data agreements with AI providers.
What You Should Know
•	Do not send protected health information (PHI), Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, or other highly sensitive data through the ChatGPT desktop app.
•	Do not blindly execute AI-generated code without reviewing it first. ChatGPT Codex can produce code with security vulnerabilities, incorrect logic, or unintended side effects.
•	Be aware of academic integrity policies. Students should consult their instructors and course syllabi regarding the acceptable use of AI coding tools in coursework and assignments.
•	Protect your credentials. Do not commit API keys, tokens, or passwords to version control. Use environment variables or secure credential stores.
Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
Account comparison
Feature	Personal ChatGPT Account	Rutgers ChatGPT Edu
Data used for model training	Yes	No
Enterprise data protections	No	Yes
Institutional support	No	Yes
Using a Rutgers-provided ChatGPT Edu subscription or the Portkey API integration is strongly recommended for any university-related work.
Understanding Costs: ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are Agentic Systems, Not a Chatbot
ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are fundamentally different from conversational AI tools like ChatGPT's own Chat option available on the web and in the desktop app, Copilot, or Gemini. Both the ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex tabs are agentic systems - meaning they can autonomously browse files, execute multi-step workflows, and chain together many operations to complete a task. A single prompt can trigger dozens or even hundreds of calls behind the scenes as GPT reasons through your request, gathers context, and produces a result.
This means ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex can consume significant tokens very quickly. Every step in its reasoning, every file it reads, and every response it generates costs tokens. A complex task that takes GPT several minutes of autonomous work can easily cost more in a single session than an entire day of conversational chatbot usage.
Usage and Rate Cards
Usage under a ChatGPT Edu subscription is metered differently depending on which module you use. Be aware of which module you are using and its associated rate card:
•	ChatGPT Codex and ChatGPT Work are subject to the Codex Rate Card.
•	ChatGPT Chat through the desktop app is subject to the ChatGPT Rate Card (Business/Enterprise/Edu).
What ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex Are Designed For
ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are purpose-built for complex, multi-step tasks where their agentic capabilities provide real value:
•	In-depth document analysis that requires cross-referencing multiple sources
•	Complex research tasks that involve reasoning across many pieces of information
•	Software development projects using the Code tab
•	Multi-stage workflows that require planning, execution, and iteration
•	Tasks that benefit from desktop automation and tool integration through Cowork
What ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are NOT Designed For
Do not use the ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex sections of the ChatGPT desktop app for tasks that a simple chatbot can handle. These tasks waste significant resources because the agentic infrastructure activates regardless of how simple your question is:
•	General knowledge questions - “What is the weather today?” or “Explain the difference between TCP and UDP”
•	Simple writing tasks - “Draft a short email to my team about the upcoming meeting”
•	Quick lookups - “How do I make hard boiled eggs?”
•	Learning and tutorials - “Explain how to get started with Python Flask”
•	Brainstorming - “Give me ideas for my research project”
For these types of tasks, use the Chat tab of the desktop app, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, or the Portkey APIs directly.
How to Get Started
There are three ways to authenticate and use the ChatGPT desktop app at Rutgers: using the ChatGPT desktop app (recommended), using the Codex CLI with your Rutgers ChatGPT Edu subscription, or configuring the Codex CLI to use the Portkey API gateway.
Option 1: Purchase a ChatGPT Edu Subscription and Download the ChatGPT Desktop App (Recommended)
The ChatGPT desktop app provides the full ChatGPT Codex experience with an integrated graphical interface. This option requires a purchased ChatGPT Edu license — it cannot be accessed using a Portkey API key.
1.	Purchase a ChatGPT Edu subscription. Visit the University Software Portal at software.rutgers.edu and search for ChatGPT Edu. Faculty and staff can purchase subscriptions for themselves or for members of their department.
2.	Download the ChatGPT desktop app. It is currently available for macOS and Windows.
3.	Launch the app and sign in. Open the ChatGPT desktop app and select Sign in with ChatGPT. Authenticate with your Rutgers ChatGPT Edu credentials: 
o	You will be redirected to the ChatGPT login page. Use the email address sign-in option and enter your Rutgers email (netid@rutgers.edu) and click Continue.
o	When prompted for how to log in, select “Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey”.
o	You will be redirected to the Rutgers Central Authentication Service (CAS) login page, login with your NetID and password.
o	You may be asked to verify it’s you by confirming the details of the login attempt. Click the Approve sign-in to proceed.
o	If this is your first time signing into the ChatGPT desktop app, it may ask for permission to access your ChatGPT account. Review the permissions and click Continue to continue.
o	You can confirm you are signed in to the Rutgers tenant by looking for the Rutgers logo and "Rutgers University" in the bottom-left corner of the app.
4.	Start using ChatGPT Codex or ChatGPT Work. Use the Projects menu item on the left to create a new project or open an existing one. To use ChatGPT Codex, click the dropdown on the top left of the application. Projects for ChatGPT Work and ChatGPT Codex are separate. Once you are ready, describe the task you want ChatGPT Codex or ChatGPT Work to perform.
Option 2: Sign In with a Rutgers ChatGPT Edu Subscription (CLI)
If you prefer working in the terminal, the Codex CLI provides access to all ChatGPT Codex features, including the latest models. This option also requires a purchased ChatGPT Edu license.
1.	Purchase a ChatGPT Edu subscription. Visit the University Software Portal at software.rutgers.edu and search for ChatGPT Edu. Faculty and staff can purchase subscriptions for themselves or for members of their department.
2.	Install Codex CLI. Open a terminal and run:
3.	npm install -g @openai/codex
Codex CLI is also available via Homebrew (brew install --cask codex) or as a direct binary download from the GitHub releases page.
4.	Create or navigate to a project directory. The Codex CLI works best when run from within a project directory that contains your codebase. You can create a new directory mkdir or navigate to an existing one cd first. You should never run codex from your home directory or any directory containing sensitive files.
5.	Launch the Codex CLI and sign in. Run codex in your terminal. You will be asked to trust the directory you are in, if you trst it tell it Yes, continue, if not choose No, quit and go to a directory you trust. On first launch, select Sign in with ChatGPT and authenticate with your Rutgers credentials:
o	You will be redirected to the ChatGPT login page. Use the email address sign-in option and enter your Rutgers email (netid@rutgers.edu) and click Continue.
o	When prompted for how to log in, select “Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey”.
o	You will be redirected to the Rutgers Central Authentication Service (CAS) login page, login with your NetID and password.
o	You may be asked to verify it’s you by confirming the details of the login attempt. Click the Approve sign-in to proceed.
o	If this is your first time signing into the Codex CLI, it may ask for permission to access your ChatGPT account. Review the permissions and click Continue to continue.
If you have already signed in through the desktop app, the CLI should automatically detect your credentials and sign you in without needing to repeat the process.
6.	Start using ChatGPT Codex. Navigate to a project directory and run codex followed by a natural language description of what you want to do. For example:
7.	codex "add input validation to the signup form"
Option 3: Use Portkey API Integration
If you do not have a ChatGPT Edu subscription, you can configure the Codex CLI and ChatGPT desktop app to route requests through Rutgers’ Portkey API gateway. This provides access to OpenAI models (and other providers) through Portkey, though some ChatGPT Codex and ChatGPT Work features that require a direct ChatGPT login may not be available.
1.	Obtain a Portkey API key. Follow the instructions in the Getting Started with Portkey guide to request access and obtain your API key from the Rutgers Account Tools Self-Service area, within the Portkey card (once you have a Portkey account activated).
2.	Install Codex CLI if needed. Open a terminal and run:
3.	npm install -g @openai/codex
4.	Create or edit the Codex CLI/ChatGPT desktop app configuration file at ~/.codex/config.toml and add a custom model provider:
5.	model_provider = "portkey"
6.	model = "@model_provider/model_name"
7.	
8.	[model_providers.portkey]
9.	name = "Portkey"
10.	base_url = "https://api.portkey.ai/v1"
11.	env_key = "PORTKEY_API_KEY"
12.	wire_api = "responses"
You can identify available models and providers for your Portkey workspace by going to the Rutgers Account Tools Self-Service area and selecting Manage API Keys in the Portkey card.
13.	Add Portkey API key to environment variables. Add the following line to your shell profile (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, etc.) with your actual API key:
14.	export PORTKEY_API_KEY="your_portkey_api_key_here"
Then reload your shell configuration with source ~/.bashrc or source ~/.zshrc.
15.	Launch the Codex CLI or ChatGPT desktop app. Run codex in your terminal and begin working. If using the ChatGPT desktop app with a Portkey API key, you may notice some slight UI differences, such as the ChatGPT Work tab not having a Chat option, and instead of seeing "Rutgers University" in the bottom right of the app, you should see "Portkey". 
o	NOTE: You may see a warning saying "Model metadata for @provider/model not found. ...this may degrade performance and cause issues." that can be ignored, it’s just because the Codex CLI doesn’t have the full metadata that it can normally receive from the OpenAI servers. From our experience, the Codex CLI still works with Portkey as a provider without any issues.
Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Be specific with your prompts. Instead of “fix the bug,” try “fix the null pointer exception in the processOrder function when the shipping address is empty.”
•	Provide context. Let ChatGPT Codex know what framework, language, or conventions your project uses.
•	Use autonomy modes. ChatGPT Codex offers configurable approval modes that control how much oversight you have before it edits files or runs commands. Start with a more cautious mode until you are comfortable.
•	Point ChatGPT Codex at tests. When possible, ask ChatGPT Codex to run your test suite after making changes so it can verify its own work.
•	Iterate on results. If the first attempt isn’t right, provide feedback and ask ChatGPT Codex to refine its approach.
•	Use the lowest-cost model for the work needed. ChatGPT Codex offers several models at different capabilities and cost tiers. The default when launching is often a high-capability model such as GPT?5.6 Sol, but simpler tasks — writing a small script, explaining a function, or fixing a typo — do not require it. Select a lower-cost model when it will suffice.
Other Access Methods
In addition to the desktop application and terminal CLI, ChatGPT Codex is available through the following (ChatGPT Edu subscription required):
•	VS Code extension - Install the Codex extension from the VS Code Extensions panel and log in with your Rutgers ChatGPT account.
•	Web interface - Use Codex Cloud at chatgpt.com/codex to run tasks in cloud sandboxes by logging in with your Rutgers ChatGPT account.
Other Free AI Tools at Rutgers
Before purchasing a ChatGPT Edu subscription, consider that Rutgers also provides free access to other AI tools, including Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. For AI-assisted coding specifically, tools like Claude Code can also be configured to work with the Portkey API gateway. The Office of Information Technology recommends exploring free alternatives unless your unit has an immediate need for a paid subscription.
Links
•	Codex - OpenAI
•	Codex CLI Documentation
•	Codex Configuration Reference
•	Codex GitHub Repository
•	ChatGPT Edu at Rutgers - Rutgers IT
•	University Software Portal
•	ChatGPT Edu FAQs
•	Getting Started with Portkey at Rutgers
•	AI at Rutgers - Office of Information Technology
•	Codex Rate Card
•	ChatGPT Rate Card (Business/Enterprise/Edu)

title: Platform and API Services Getting Started with Claude Code (Terminal CLI)
body:
Claude Code is Anthropic’s AI-powered coding assistant that runs directly in your terminal. It can read and edit files, run commands, search your codebase, interact with Git, and help you build, debug, and refactor code through natural language conversation. By integrating Portkey with Claude Code, you can use Claude’s AI capabilities while routing all requests through Rutgers’ enterprise Portkey gateway, ensuring your data is protected and usage is tracked.
This guide walks you through installing Claude Code and configuring it to work with your Rutgers Portkey account in the terminal. If you prefer to use Claude Code within VS Code, see Getting Started with the Claude Code VS Code Extension instead.
Table of Contents
•	Appropriate Use
•	Safety and Data Protection 
o	What You Should Know
•	Understanding Costs: Claude Code Is an Agentic System, Not a Chatbot 
o	What Claude Code Is Designed For
o	What Claude Code Is NOT Designed For
o	Monitoring Your Usage
•	Installation 
o	Step 1: Install Claude Code
o	Step 2: Initialize Claude Code
o	Step 3: Configure Portkey Connection
o	Step 4: Bypass the Onboarding Process
o	Step 5: Test Your Setup
•	Configuration File Reference
•	Useful Slash Commands
•	Known Limitations
•	Links
Appropriate Use
Claude Code is a powerful tool for software development and technical work:
•	Writing code - Generate functions, classes, scripts, and entire project structures from natural language descriptions.
•	Debugging - Describe a bug or error message and let Claude help identify and fix the issue.
•	Refactoring - Ask Claude to improve code quality, modernize patterns, or restructure files.
•	Code review - Get feedback on your code’s quality, security, and maintainability.
•	Learning - Ask Claude to explain code, concepts, or design patterns.
As with all AI tools, always review code generated by Claude before running or deploying it. AI-generated code can contain bugs, security vulnerabilities, or incorrect logic.
Safety and Data Protection
When Claude Code is configured to use Rutgers’ Portkey gateway, all API requests are routed through the university’s enterprise instance:
•	Your code and conversations are not used to train AI models.
•	API usage is tracked for accounting purposes through the Portkey for auditing and cost management.
What You Should Know
•	Do not use Claude Code on repositories that contain highly sensitive data, such as PHI, Social Security numbers, or financial credentials.
•	Review all code changes before accepting them. Claude Code will ask for your approval before modifying files.
•	Protect your Portkey API key. If your key is compromised, contact your administrator immediately to rotate it.
•	Do not start Claude Code in your home directory. Always navigate to a specific project directory first (see warning below).
Understanding Costs: Claude Code Is an Agentic System, Not a Chatbot
Claude Code is fundamentally different from conversational AI tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini. It is an agentic system - meaning it autonomously reads files, runs commands, searches your codebase, makes edits, and chains together multiple operations to complete a task. A single prompt can trigger dozens or even hundreds of API calls behind the scenes as Claude explores your project, plans an approach, and implements changes.
This means Claude Code can consume significant API credits very quickly. Every file it reads, every search it runs, and every response it generates costs tokens. A complex task that takes Claude several minutes of autonomous work can easily cost more in a single session than an entire day of conversational chatbot usage.
What Claude Code Is Designed For
Claude Code is purpose-built for complex, multi-step software development tasks where its agentic capabilities provide real value:
•	Implementing a new feature across multiple files in a codebase
•	Debugging a complex issue that requires reading and tracing code across many files
•	Refactoring an entire module or migrating a codebase to a new pattern
•	Setting up a project with build configuration, tests, and CI/CD pipelines
•	Reviewing a pull request and providing detailed, code-aware feedback
What Claude Code Is NOT Designed For
Do not use Claude Code for tasks that a simple chatbot can handle. These tasks waste significant resources because Claude Code’s agentic infrastructure activates regardless of how simple your question is:
•	General knowledge questions - “What is the weather today?” or “Explain the difference between TCP and UDP”
•	Simple code snippets - “Write me a quick Python script to convert CSV to JSON”
•	Learning and tutorials - “Explain how to get started with Python Flask”
•	Writing and editing - “Draft an email to my team about the upcoming meeting”
•	Brainstorming - “Give me ideas for my research project”
For these types of tasks, use ChatGPT Edu, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, or the Portkey APIs directly - they are far more cost-effective for conversational and single-turn tasks.
Monitoring Your Usage
Keep an eye on your API spending by logging into the Rutgers Account Tools Self-Service area and looking for your Portkey card (once you have a Portkey account). If you are unsure whether a task warrants using Claude Code, consider whether the task requires Claude to autonomously explore and modify your codebase. If it does not, use a less expensive tool.
Installation
Step 1: Install Claude Code
Open your terminal and run:
macOS / Linux:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Windows (PowerShell):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
After installation, the installer may instruct you to add Claude to your PATH by modifying your .bashrc or .zshrc file. Follow the on-screen instructions - it will typically be a simple echo command to append to your shell configuration file.
For more installation options, see the Claude Code Quickstart documentation.
Step 2: Initialize Claude Code
Run the following command to initialize Claude Code without starting an interactive session:
claude --init-only
Step 3: Configure Portkey Connection
Create or edit the global settings file at ~/.claude/settings.json with the following content:
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "theme": "dark",
  "editor": "code",
  "env": {
    "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://api.portkey.ai",
    "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "YOUR_PORTKEY_API_KEY",
    "ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS": "x-portkey-api-key: YOUR_PORTKEY_API_KEY\nx-portkey-provider: @model_provider",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "model_name1",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "model_name2",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "model_name3"
  },
  "model": "model_name1"
}
Replace both instances of YOUR_PORTKEY_API_KEY with your actual Portkey API key from the Rutgers Account Tools Self-Service area, within the Portkey card (once you have a Portkey account activated). You can also retrieve model providers and model names from this same card.
Configuration Explained
Settings explanations
Setting	Purpose
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL	Redirects Claude Code to send requests through Portkey instead of directly to Anthropic.
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN	Authenticates your requests with Portkey.
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS	Passes your Portkey API key and specifies the @claude-models provider for routing.
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL	Specifies which Claude model to use for each tier (Sonnet, Opus, Haiku).
model	Sets the default model Claude Code uses for conversations.
Step 4: Bypass the Onboarding Process
Since you are authenticating through Portkey rather than an Anthropic account, you need to skip Claude Code’s standard onboarding flow. Edit the file ~/.claude.json and add the following line somewhere in the JSON object:
"hasCompletedOnboarding": true,
For example, if your ~/.claude.json looks like this:
{
  "someExistingSetting": "value"
}
Change it to:
{
  "someExistingSetting": "value",
  "hasCompletedOnboarding": true
}
Step 5: Test Your Setup
Important: Never start Claude Code from your home directory. Always create or navigate to a project directory first.
mkdir ~/testing
cd ~/testing
claude
Once Claude Code starts, try a simple prompt to verify everything is working:
Create a simple hello world python script in a file named helloworld.py
If Claude successfully generates the file, your Portkey integration is configured correctly.
Configuration File Reference
Claude Code uses a hierarchy of configuration files that let you manage settings at different levels:
File explanations
File	Path	Purpose
Global settings	~/.claude/settings.json	Settings that apply to every project. This is where your Portkey configuration lives.
Project settings	your-project/.claude/settings.json	Settings shared with your team (usually committed to Git).
Local project overrides	your-project/.claude/settings.local.json	Personal overrides for a specific project (make sure your .gitignore file ignores this so it is not commited to Git).
Useful Slash Commands
Once inside Claude Code, you can use slash commands to control your session:
List of commands
Command	Description
/help	Show available commands
/clear	Clear conversation history
/resume	Resume a previous conversation
/compact	Condense the current conversation to save context
/model	Change the current model
For a complete list, see the Claude Code Commands documentation.
Known Limitations
Since you are connecting through Portkey rather than signing into a Claude account with a Pro or Max subscription, the following limitations apply:
•	Remote Control is not available. Features that require a direct Anthropic account connection (such as Remote Control for collaborative sessions) will not work through Portkey.
•	Slack integration is not available. The Slack app requires a direct connection to an Anthropic account and cannot be used with Portkey.
•	Some account-specific features may be unavailable. Features tied to Anthropic subscription tiers may not be accessible when routing through a third-party API gateway.
•	No voice dictation. Voice dictation streams your recorded audio to Anthropic’s servers for transcription. Audio is not processed locally. The speech-to-text service is only available when you authenticate with a Claude.ai account.
Links
•	Claude Code Quickstart
•	Claude Code Commands Reference
•	Portkey Dashboard
•	Getting Started with Portkey at Rutgers
•	Getting Started with the Claude Code VS Code Extension
•	Getting Started with Claude Desktop
•	AI at Rutgers - Office of Information Technology

title: Platform and API Services Getting Started with Claude Desktop
body:
Claude Desktop is Anthropic’s native application for macOS and Windows that brings Claude’s AI capabilities to your desktop. It provides three primary modes:
•	Chat - A traditional conversational AI interface for direct interaction with Claude.
NOTE: When using third-party inference, the Chat tab is not available - only the Cowork and Code tabs are accessible. The Chat tab requires a direct Anthropic account.
•	Cowork - An autonomous agent that can execute multi-step knowledge work tasks on your behalf, including file operations, web browsing, and desktop automation - without requiring terminal expertise.
•	Code - An integrated development environment for AI-powered software development, debugging, and code review.
By configuring Claude Desktop to use a third-party inference provider like Portkey, all AI requests are routed through Rutgers’ enterprise gateway instead of Anthropic’s servers. This ensures your conversations and data remain under university data protection agreements while giving you access to Claude’s full capabilities.
This deployment mode - called “Cowork on 3P (Third Party)” - is designed for organizations that need to control where their data flows. Conversations are stored locally on your device, and only model inference requests are sent through your configured provider (in this case, Portkey).
Table of Contents
•	Appropriate Use 
o	Cowork
o	Code
o	General Conversations
•	Safety and Data Protection 
o	What You Should Know
•	Understanding Costs: Claude Desktop Is an Agentic System, Not a Chatbot 
o	What Claude Desktop Is Designed For
o	What Claude Desktop Is NOT Designed For
o	Monitoring Your Usage
•	System Requirements
•	Installation and Setup 
o	Step 1: Download Claude Desktop
o	Step 2: Enable Developer Mode
o	Step 3: Configure Third-Party Inference
o	Step 4: Apply Configuration
o	Step 5: Verify Your Setup
•	Architecture Overview
•	Telemetry Data
•	Known Limitations
•	Links
Appropriate Use
Cowork
The Cowork tab is an agentic workspace for complex knowledge work. Claude can autonomously work through multi-step tasks, interact with files on your computer, and use connectors to integrate with tools like Slack and Chrome. Use it for:
•	Document analysis - Upload files and documents for Claude to analyze, summarize, cross-reference, and discuss.
•	Research and synthesis - Explore topics, synthesize information from multiple sources, and organize findings.
•	Project planning - Break down complex tasks, outline approaches, and work through problems step by step.
•	Writing and editing - Draft, revise, and refine documents with Claude working autonomously through multiple rounds.
•	Data processing - Claude can run code in an isolated environment to process data, generate visualizations, and produce reports.
Code
The Code tab provides an AI-powered development workspace. Use it for:
•	Software development - Build, debug, and refactor code with AI assistance.
•	Code review - Get feedback on code quality, security, and best practices.
General Conversations
For simple questions and quick tasks that don’t require agentic capabilities, consider using ChatGPT Edu, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, or the Portkey APIs directly instead - they are far more cost-effective for conversational and single-turn tasks.
As with all AI tools, always review AI-generated content for accuracy before using it in any official capacity.
Safety and Data Protection
When Claude Desktop is configured to route through Rutgers’ Portkey gateway:
•	Your conversations are stored locally on your device, not on Anthropic’s servers.
•	Your data is not used to train AI models. The enterprise agreements ensure your inputs and outputs are protected.
•	Only inference requests are sent through Portkey. The application itself runs locally - only conversation data is transmitted to Portkey.
•	Telemetry data (crash reports, analytics) sent to Anthropic is scrubbed of conversation and user data and can be disabled entirely if needed.
What You Should Know
•	Do not enter protected health information (PHI), Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, or other highly sensitive data into Claude Desktop.
•	Review AI-generated content carefully. Claude can produce plausible-sounding but incorrect information.
•	Protect your configuration. Your Portkey API key is stored in your system’s managed configuration. Do not share configuration files that contain your API key.
Understanding Costs: Claude Desktop Is an Agentic System, Not a Chatbot
Claude Desktop is fundamentally different from conversational AI tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini. Both the Cowork and Code tabs are agentic systems - meaning they can autonomously browse files, execute multi-step workflows, and chain together many operations to complete a task. A single prompt can trigger dozens or even hundreds of API calls behind the scenes as Claude reasons through your request, gathers context, and produces a result.
This means Claude Desktop can consume significant API credits very quickly. Every step in its reasoning, every file it reads, and every response it generates costs tokens. A complex task that takes Claude several minutes of autonomous work can easily cost more in a single session than an entire day of conversational chatbot usage.
What Claude Desktop Is Designed For
Claude Desktop is purpose-built for complex, multi-step tasks where its agentic capabilities provide real value:
•	In-depth document analysis that requires cross-referencing multiple sources
•	Complex research tasks that involve reasoning across many pieces of information
•	Software development projects using the Code tab
•	Multi-stage workflows that require planning, execution, and iteration
•	Tasks that benefit from desktop automation and tool integration through Cowork
What Claude Desktop Is NOT Designed For
Do not use Claude Desktop for tasks that a simple chatbot can handle. These tasks waste significant resources because the agentic infrastructure activates regardless of how simple your question is:
•	General knowledge questions - “What is the weather today?” or “Explain the difference between TCP and UDP”
•	Simple writing tasks - “Draft a short email to my team about the upcoming meeting”
•	Quick lookups - “How do I make hard boiled eggs?”
•	Learning and tutorials - “Explain how to get started with Python Flask”
•	Brainstorming - “Give me ideas for my research project”
For these types of tasks, use ChatGPT Edu, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, or the Portkey APIs directly.
Monitoring Your Usage
Keep an eye on your API spending by logging into the Rutgers Account Tools Self-Service area and looking for your Portkey card (once you have a Portkey account). If you are unsure whether a task warrants using Claude Desktop, ask yourself: Does this task require Claude to autonomously reason through multiple steps, read files, or execute a multi-part workflow? If not, use a less expensive tool.
System Requirements
•	macOS: Version 13.0 (Ventura) or later
•	Windows: Windows 10 or Windows 11
•	Portkey credentials: A Rutgers Portkey API key from app.portkey.ai
Installation and Setup
Step 1: Download Claude Desktop
1.	Go to claude.com/download and download the installer for your operating system.
2.	macOS: Open the .dmg file and drag Claude.app to your Applications folder.
3.	Windows: Run the .msix installer and follow the prompts.
Step 2: Enable Developer Mode
After installing, launch the Claude Desktop application. Do not sign in with an Anthropic account. Instead:
1.	Go to Help > Troubleshooting in the menu bar.
2.	Click Enable Developer Mode.
3.	A new Developer menu will appear.
Step 3: Configure Third-Party Inference
1.	Go to Developer > Configure third-party inference in the menu bar.
2.	The setup interface will appear, with fields to configure your inference provider.
3.	Configure the following settings:
Values for fields
Field	Value
Connection	Gateway
Gateway Base URL	https://api.portkey.ai
Credential kind	Static API key
Gateway API Key	Your Portkey API key
Gateway auth scheme	bearer
Custom inference headers	x-portkey-api-key: YOUR_PORTKEY_API_KEY and x-portkey-provider: @model_provider
Model discovery	Turn the slider to OFF. This setting does not work with Portkey.
Model list (add these)	model_name1, model_name2, model_name3
Offer 1M-context variant	If the model you're configuring supports this feature, you may toggle the slider. Otherwise, leave it off.
Tier alias	Optional configuration to select models faster without having to remember versions. Select the appropriate option if desired.
Default for tier	If setting up multiple models in the same class (ex. Opus 4.6 and Opus 4.8), you may wish to set one as the default for when you use the above tier alias.
Disable Claude.ai sign-in	Turn the slider to OFF. You will have to search for this setting as it is not in the "Connection" tab.
Replace YOUR_PORTKEY_API_KEY with your actual Portkey API key from the Rutgers Account Tools Self-Service area, within the Portkey card (once you have a Portkey account activated). You can also retrieve model providers and model names from this same card.
Step 4: Apply Configuration
Press the Apply locally button to save your changes.
Step 5: Verify Your Setup
After applying the configuration, restart Claude Desktop. If configured correctly:
•	You will see Cowork and Code tabs in the application.
•	There will be no Chat tab (the Chat tab requires a direct Anthropic account and is not available with third-party inference).
•	You will be able to start a conversation and receive responses routed through Portkey.
Try a simple prompt to verify:
Hello! Can you confirm you're working correctly?
If you receive a response, your Portkey integration is configured correctly.
Architecture Overview
When using Claude Desktop with Portkey, the data flow is:
Your Device (Claude Desktop) -> Portkey Gateway (api.portkey.ai) -> Claude AI Models -> Portkey -> Your Device
Component locations
Component	Where It Runs
Claude Desktop application	Locally on your device
Conversation storage	Locally on your device
Model inference	Routed through Portkey to AI providers
Telemetry (optional)	Anthropic (scrubbed of conversation data)
This architecture ensures that your conversation data never leaves your device except as inference requests to the configured gateway.
Telemetry Data
Anthropic's telemetry data never includes your prompts or responses; it only includes metrics such as token usage, crash reports, and general OS information.  If you would like to completely disable all telemetry, you'll need to do a little search and manual editing of config files. First, completely close the Claude Desktop.
Navigate to the ~/Library/Application Support/Claude-3p/configLibrary/ folder in Finder and open the _meta.json file to find the appliedId value, which contains the filename that we need to open next. The file will look something like abcd2345-a322-b321-234b-723abcdef234.json, open that file, and we want to add 4 lines right about the inferenceModels line:
Do the following:
  "disableEssentialTelemetry": true,
  "disableNonessentialTelemetry": true,
  "disableNonessentialServices": true,
  "disableAutoUpdates": true,
When you restart Claude Desktop, all telemetry data will be disabled.
Known Limitations
Since you are using Claude Desktop via a third-party provider (Portkey) rather than a standard Anthropic account:
•	No Chat tab. The Chat experience requires a direct Anthropic account and is not available in third-party inference mode.
•	No Anthropic account login. Authentication is handled through your Portkey API key, not an Anthropic account.
•	No plugin support. Plugin support is not possible when configuration is through an organization, which we do not have available at this time.
•	Some features may be unavailable. Features that require Anthropic’s cloud infrastructure (such as the skills marketplace) may not be available in third-party deployment mode.
•	Configuration is managed locally or via MDM. There is no web-based admin console - settings are applied through configuration files or mobile device management.
