title: Phone Support Call forwarding on Cisco phones
body:
All VoIP telephone users can forward their desk phones to a remote number of their choice in North America. Detailed training instructions for your phone can be found in the Using Cisco Phones article. Please note you must be on the Rutgers Network (or VPN) to access the training.
If you are not a Rutgers VoIP customer, please contact the Voice help desk by opening a ticket in the Voice Services Request Tool to discuss your available options.
Forward all calls, via the online portal
You must be on the Rutgers Network (or VPN) in order to access the Cisco Unified Communications Self-Care Portal.
1.	Navigate to the Cisco Unified Communications Self Care Portal 
2.	Login using your credentials.
3.	From the Voice Tab Select Call Forwarding
4.	Check Forward all calls to: box and enter the call forward target number exactly as you would dial it from your phone.
5.	Please note that there are advanced features available.
6.	Once you have completed entering your data click Save to enable the Call Forward.
Call forward can be turned off by simply deselecting the “Forward all calls to:” box and clicking Save.
Forward All Calls at the Phone
“Forward All” allows you to forward calls on your phone to another number.
1.	Press the Forward All softkey.
2.	Then enter the call forward target phone number exactly as you would dial it from your phone.
3.	To verify that your calls are forwarded, look for the “Forward All” icon in the line label, and the forwarding information in the header.
Cancel Call Forwarding at the Phone
Press the Forward Off softkey.
Voicemails to Email (.wav)
Another option that supports working remotely is having voicemails sent to your email. Some of the phone systems support this feature. Please submit a voice ticket to enable this feature. For more information, follow the instructions on How to access your voicemail remotely.

title: and Mobile Device Support Change your AirDrop settings to prevent unsolicited images and files
body:
AirDrop is a fast and convenient way to share photos, videos, and files with other Apple device users. It does so wirelessly via Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, which makes it very easy to use, but also can leave your device exposed to potentially unsolicited images and files. By design, it will display a preview of the item before you agree to receive it or reject it. You will have to view every item sent to you by anyone who has permission to do so and is within range of your device, which makes it an easy target for unwanted images and files. 
There are two active permission settings for AirDrop:
•	You can set it to accept shares from anyone.
•	Or only from people in your contacts who are saved.
Alternatively, you can completely turn off the feature. You can use these settings to ensure you don't become the unwitting victim of an unsolicited AirDrop share. It should be turned off completely or limited to Contacts Only whenever possible.
See Apple’s instructions on changing your AirDrop settings on your iPhone/iPad, or on a Mac.

title: and Mobile Device Support Retrieving MAC Addresses
body:
Providing your MAC addresses may be necessary to troubleshoot wired and wireless issues properly or to sign up for certain services. Locating a device's MAC address is dependent on its manufacturer. Below is a list of commonly used devices and instructions for finding their MAC addresses.
*An important note is that the wired MAC address may sometimes be referred to as the RJ45 MAC address.
MacOS
1.	Open System Preferences > Network
2.	Select Ethernet or Wi-Fi depending on connection type, then click Advanced
3.	Select the Hardware tab; it will be listed as MAC Address
Windows
1.	Run command prompt (cmd)
2.	Type ipconfig/all and select Enter (on the keyboard)
3.	Scroll down to Ethernet or Wireless adapters
4.	It will be listed as Physical Address
Chromebooks
1.	If you haven't yet, sign in to your Chromebook.
2.	At the bottom right, select the time.
3.	Select the Wi-Fi network Error! Filename not specified..
4.	At the top of the box, select Information Error! Filename not specified..
5.	You'll see your Chromebook's IP address and IPv6 address. Your MAC address is labeled "Wi-Fi."
Alternate method for Windows 10
1.	Open Settings from the Start menu
2.	Select Network and Internet
3.	Select View your network properties
4.	The MAC address is listed as Physical Address (MAC)
PlayStation 4
1.	On the main menu, navigate to Settings.
2.	Click Network.
3.	Navigate to View Connection Status.
4.	Here you will see the Wifi MAC Address and the Ethernet MAC Address.
5.	For 802.1x MAC Address Bypass, we will need the Ethernet MAC Address.
Xbox One
1.	Open the Guide
2.	Select Settings
3.	Select Network
4.	Select Advanced Settings
5.	The addresses should be labeled Wired MAC and Wireless MAC
Apple TV
1.	Select Settings
2.	Select General
3.	Select Network
4.	The MAC address will be listed as Ethernet Address
Android TV
1.	Select Settings
2.	Select Network
3.	Select Status
4.	The MAC Address will be listed here
Roku
1.	The MAC address is printed on the bottom or back of the Roku player
2.	Alternatively, from the Roku home screen, select Settings > Network > Wired (Ethernet)
3.	Secret Menu option for Roku 3 or later (use the following key combination): Home, Home, Home, Home, Home, FF, FF, FF, RW, RW
Amazon Fire Stick
1.	From the Main Menu, go to Settings
2.	Select System
3.	Go to About
4.	Toggle down to Network. Look for the MAC Address (Wi-Fi) on the right
Nintendo Switch
1.	Select System Settings from the home menu.
2.	Scroll down through the menu and select Internet.
3.	The MAC address will be listed under System MAC Address.
4.	Note: If you want to connect via an Ethernet cable, you will need a certified Nintendo adapter. If you have this, then you will need to use the adapter's MAC address rather than the switch's MAC address. The easiest way to get the MAC address (if it is not hardcoded into the adapter) is to have the user plug it into a Windows machine. Go to the command prompt and type ipconfig/all, scroll down until you see the adapter, and the MAC address should be listed as the physical address.

title: and Mobile Device Support Windows 10 End of Life (EOL) & Upgrade to Windows 11 - FAQ
body:
Microsoft has announced the official End of Life (EOL) date for Windows 10 as October 14, 2025. After this date, devices running Windows 10 will no longer receive security updates or technical support from Microsoft. Rutgers University is preparing for this transition and has developed a plan to upgrade eligible devices to Windows 11.
This FAQ is intended to provide guidance for faculty, staff, and students regarding the upcoming changes.
Table of Contents
•	General Windows 10 End of Life 
o	When is Windows 10 reaching end of life?
o	What does "end of life" mean for Windows 10?
o	Why is Microsoft ending support for Windows 10?
o	What happens if I continue using Windows 10 after the end-of-life date?
o	Is there any way to extend Windows 10 support?
•	Upgrade to Windows 11 
o	Am I required to upgrade to Windows 11?
o	How do I know if my computer can run Windows 11?
o	What are the minimum hardware requirements for Windows 11?
o	Will I lose my files or programs during the upgrade?
o	Can I upgrade remotely?
o	Are there any known compatibility issues with Rutgers software?
•	University-Managed Devices 
o	Will Rutgers upgrade university devices automatically?
o	Who do I contact for help upgrading my Rutgers-owned device?
o	Can I delay the upgrade?
o	Will the upgrade be done through KACE, or another tool?
•	Personally-Owned Devices (BYOD) 
o	Does this affect my personal computer?
o	Is Windows 11 free?
o	Will Extended Security Updates (ESU) be available for personal devices? 
•	Security and Compliance 
o	Is it a security risk to stay on Windows 10?
o	Will outdated devices be blocked from the Rutgers network?
o	How does this relate to university compliance?
•	IT Administrators 
o	As the IT Administrator for my department, how do I deploy the upgrade through KACE? 
•	Additional Help
General Windows 10 End of Life
When is Windows 10 reaching end of life?
Microsoft will officially end support for Windows 10 on October 14, 2025.
What does "end of life" mean for Windows 10?
It means Microsoft will no longer provide security updates, bug fixes, or technical support. This could expose devices to security vulnerabilities.
Why is Microsoft ending support for Windows 10?
Microsoft follows a product lifecycle policy. Windows 10 was released in 2015 and is being phased out in favor of Windows 11, which offers improved performance, security, and support for modern hardware.
What happens if I continue using Windows 10 after the end-of-life date?
Your device will still work, but it will no longer receive security updates, leaving it vulnerable to threats. Some university systems may eventually block unsupported operating systems from the network.
Is there any way to extend Windows 10 support?
Windows 10 Extended Security Updates (ESU) will be available at no cost for university-owned devices in the fall. In the meantime, it's strongly recommended to upgrade any devices capable of running Windows 11 to ensure continued support and access to the latest features and security updates.
Upgrade to Windows 11
Am I required to upgrade to Windows 11?
All university-managed Windows devices must be upgraded or install the ESU patch before the EOL deadline to ensure compliance and security.
How do I know if my computer can run Windows 11?
You can check compatibility using the PC Health Check Tool. Most devices from 2019 onward are compatible.
What are the minimum hardware requirements for Windows 11?
Requirements include a compatible 64-bit CPU, 4GB RAM, 64GB storage, TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, and UEFI firmware.
Will I lose my files or programs during the upgrade?
No, the upgrade is designed to retain your files and installed applications. However, it is recommended to back up your data before proceeding.
Can I upgrade remotely?
Yes. The upgrade can be delivered through managed tools like KACE.
Are there any known compatibility issues with Rutgers software?
Most supported university software is compatible. If you rely on niche or lab-specific tools, please contact your department's IT support to verify compatibility.
University-Managed Devices
Will Rutgers upgrade university devices automatically?
Yes. The upgrade will be scheduled by your local IT support team. You may receive notifications or prompts depending on the configuration.
Who do I contact for help upgrading my Rutgers-owned device?
Contact your department's IT support or submit a request through the IT Help Portal.
Can I delay the upgrade?
Short-term deferrals may be granted for critical use cases. Contact your department's IT support for exceptions.
Will the upgrade be done through KACE, or another tool?
Most upgrades will be handled via KACE, depending on your device's management group.
Personally-Owned Devices (BYOD)
Does this affect my personal computer?
Not directly. However, you are encouraged to upgrade to Windows 11 to maintain a secure and supported environment.
Is Windows 11 free?
Yes, if you have a valid Windows 10 license on your device. You can upgrade through Microsoft directly. 
Will Extended Security Updates (ESU) be available for personal devices?
No. ESU cannot be licensed for personal use. 
Security and Compliance
Is it a security risk to stay on Windows 10?
Yes. Devices that no longer receive security updates are highly vulnerable to malware and unauthorized access.
Will outdated devices be blocked from the Rutgers network?
This may happen post-EOL. Policies are under review and will be communicated closer to the cutoff date.
How does this relate to university compliance?
Using unsupported software violates Rutgers IT security standards. Upgrading to Windows 11 ensures compliance with data protection and cybersecurity policies.
IT Administrators
As the IT Administrator for my department, how do I deploy the upgrade through KACE? 
Follow the guide for updating Windows features through KACE. 
Additional Help
If you have questions not listed here, or you need help planning your upgrade, please contact your department's IT support or submit a ticket on the IT Help Portal.

title: Accessibility IT Accessibility Purchasing Process
body:
For all purchases with the commodity code IT Software, purchasers must submit the Accessibility Purchasing Form.
Immediately after you submit this form, you will receive a copy of your EIT Acknowledgement Agreement. This states that you understand your purchase may not be accessible and will work with the appropriate University units should an individual with a disability require an alternate means of accessing the application.
Within 5-10 business days after submitting the form, the Office of Information Technology Accessibility (OITA) will review your request and place it into one of four categories based on several factors, including overall risk to the University.
If it falls into one of these 3 categories, your purchase is approved.
•	Low - No Audit
•	Medium - No Audit
•	High -  Full Audit
If it falls into this category, your purchase is on hold:
•	High - Purchase on hold
If the exposure level to the University is low, you may attach the email you received to the requisition and proceed with the purchase. No further action will be needed.
If the exposure level is found to be high, in most cases the purchase will proceed under the condition that a full audit by OITA be conducted before the next renewal. The email you receive will contain an outline of all your next steps.
The OITA office reserves the right to stop any purchase if we find the risk level too high or if an individual with a disability is likely to be negatively impacted by the purchase.

title: Accessibility Rutgers Digital Accessibility Policies
body:
To provide more accessible services, Rutgers has instituted a Web Accessibility policy and is generating an Online Course Accessibility policy. These policies encompass the regulatory principles the university seeks to adhere to to increase accessibility at Rutgers.
70.1.5 World Wide Web Accessibility Policy (PDF)
The Rutgers World Wide Web Accessibility Policy defines the standards for the accessibility and usability of web-based information and services to create an inclusive environment for students, faculty, and staff to invest in the usability of our web resources and to proactively comply with federal regulations and laws. All web pages newly created, redesigned, or modified by the University, any of its units, or any of its faculty must comply with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA. For more information on conformance and success criteria for the guidelines, see How to Meet WCAG (Quick Reference).
80.1.7 Website Policy (PDF)
The Rutgers Website Policy governs all Rutgers websites. This policy explains how websites must behave regarding educational materials, advertising, fundraising, links, administration, and related matters to ensure our web presence is available to the widest possible audience and is responsibly maintained.
For a full list of all University policies, please visit our University Policy Library.

title: Accessibility Rutgers Minimum Digital Accessibility Standards
body:
Rutgers is committed to ensuring that everyone in our Rutgers family can access all the tools, resources, and experiences Rutgers has to offer. We remain actively engaged with our campus partners, both internally and externally, to ensure compliance with all federal, state, and local laws. This includes but is not limited to: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
These standards operate in conjunction with the following policies here at Rutgers:
70.1.5- World Wide Web Accessibility Policy
Web Standards
All web content must meet the minimum WCAG 2.1 AA threshold.  More information on the W3Cs Web Content Accessibility Guidelines can be found on their site.
Additional Training is offered through OITA and can be booked via appointment. Please email accessibility-support@rutgers.edu to set up a training.
Document Standards
All documents (PDFs, DOCX, PPTX, etc.) should conform to the WCAG standard above, where applicable. While WCAG was written specifically for web content, its tenets and foundations can be applied to all document types.

title: Accessibility Understanding an IT Accessibility Review
body:
We recommend you read the understanding WCAG article before reading this document.
Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT)
Accessibility reviews can take many forms for a company; the most common is a VPAT. This document reports the extent to which the product meets each WCAG Conformance Standard.
These are completed either by the company or an outside agency. In general, third-party companies (unbiased) like Deque or Level Access provide honest, high-quality reviews. That is preferred over internal reviews, which tend to be skewed towards higher ratings.
The ratings used to describe the Conformance Levels are defined as follows:
•	Supports: The product's functionality has at least one method that meets the criterion without known defects or meets with equivalent facilitation.
•	Partially Supports: Some of the product's functionality does not meet the criterion.
•	Does Not Support: Most product functionality does not meet the criterion.
•	Not Applicable: The criterion is not relevant to the product.
•	Not Evaluated: The product has not been evaluated against the criterion. This can be used only in WCAG 2.0 Level AAA.
Usability Testing
Sometimes also referred to as User Experience testing, in the context of accessibility, this measures how easily a person can navigate and interact with a website using their assistive technology. In most cases, these tests are conducted using a screen reader to measure how easy it is to use the site with a keyboard only.
Accessibility Roadmaps
Companies need to continually review their software to ensure it remains usable for individuals with disabilities and remains compliant with WCAG standards. When issues are found, those should be put onto a ‘roadmap’. This document outlines the issue and a timeline for when it will be fixed.

title: Accessibility Understanding Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)
body:
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the prevailing authority on accessibility standards. It is developed in collaboration with individuals and organizations worldwide, with the goal of creating a universally accepted technical standard for web accessibility.
5 things to know about WCAG
1.	The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines were created by a group called the W3C. It is one of several guidelines that outline the requirements for making the web accessible. There are other guidelines for making browsers/browser extensions accessible, content creation tools like WordPress accessible, as well as specifications for accessible audio and video, to name a few examples. WCAG is one piece of a larger puzzle.
2.	WCAG is divided into 4 Principles (which you can think of as categories): 
o	Perceivable: Users must be able to perceive the information being presented (it can't be invisible to all of their senses).
o	Operable: Users must be able to operate the interface (the interface cannot require interaction that a user cannot perform).
o	Understandable: Users must be able to understand the information and the user interface (its content and operation cannot be beyond their understanding).
o	Robust: Users must be able to access the content as technologies advance (as technologies and user agents evolve, the content should remain accessible).
3.	Within those Principles, there are guidelines and conformance standards. For example, we can imagine a deaf or hard-of-hearing individual who needs to listen to a recorded lecture. To meet the principle of being perceivable, there must be an alternate means for the user to obtain that information. In this case, the conformance standard requires us to provide a text alternative, such as captions or a transcript.
4.	WCAG uses a good, better, best model, meaning each standard is assigned a grade. To conform to the better standards (also known as AA), you need to conform to all the standards graded under good (level A) as well as all those graded as better (level AA). 
5.	WCAG is constantly evolving. As the internet and the tools we use evolve, so must the guidelines. Often, you'll hear a version number, i.e., WCAG 2.0, to indicate which version your company has adopted as its standard.
See our minimum digital accessibility standards to learn more about the WCAG version Rutgers has adopted.
To learn more about WCAG, check out these sites:
•	Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) Overview by W3C WAI
•	Understanding the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines by Mozilla
•	Web Content Accessibility Guidelines – What Is WCAG? by Essential Accessibility

title: Classroom Services RUN: Classroom Wireless Success Steps
body:
University-supported classrooms at RU-N have the wireless infrastructure necessary to provide excellent WiFi coverage for all students and faculty. However, even the best wireless network will have its performance impacted by the use and configuration of students' devices. 
Instructors and their students can take steps to minimize connectivity issues during the in-class administration of assessments and other instructional activities that depend on the wireless network (e.g., class polls). 
Classroom Wireless Success Steps before in-class assessment or activity: 
1.	Faculty should notify students that they will need a laptop or tablet for the course, and students need to configure their devices to use the RUWireless Secure network.? If students have any issues, they should contact the RUN-IT Service Center.
2.	Students should ensure they can successfully connect to RUWireless Secure BEFORE the day of the exam or activity. The RUWireless Guest network has bandwidth and security restrictions that negatively impact students using that network in the classrooms.
3.	Students must ensure their computer's operating system is up to date.
4.	If faculty plan to use the classroom wireless for an assessment, they should schedule a practice session before the actual assessment so that students can test and verify their devices. 
Classroom Wireless Success Steps during an exam or activity: 
1.	Ask students to close all other programs and applications on their devices while taking the exam.
2.	Do not ask students to download software or other large files that may be associated with the exam at the same time as the exam. Preferably, this would be done ahead of the exam.
3.	Have a paper version of the assessment available if a student has an issue with their device during the exam. 
 For more information about troubleshooting Rutgers University's wireless connectivity, please refer to the guide on how to connect to RUWireless Secure. 
 You can also contact the RUN-IT Service Center.

title: Instructions for installing eduroam
body:
eduroam enables all Rutgers University students, faculty, staff, and emeriti to utilize free and secure wireless service when visiting an eduroam (education roaming) member university, and allows visitors from member universities to access the service when visiting Rutgers. Most Big 10 schools are participating members of the eduroam consortium. Additionally, numerous other universities, research centers, and libraries worldwide are members.
The eduroam network is available at participating institutions in over 106 territories worldwide. A full list of participating institutions in the US can be found on the eduroam-US web page. To use eduroam, you will need a WiFi (802.11b/g/n) enabled device such as a laptop, tablet, or smartphone.
1.	Rutgers University faculty, staff, students, and emeriti must download the eduroam installer. 
2.	Run the installer and provide your NetID and NetID password when prompted. 
3.	Test connecting to the eduroam network while at Rutgers. 
4.	Afterward, at another institution, you can select the eduroam wireless network on your device’s wireless connection settings and log in using the following credentials: 
o	Username = NetID@rutgers.edu
o	Password = NetID password
Tips
•	Once you have used the installer to configure your device, you can connect to wireless networks named "eduroam" at any participating institution. Before you leave Rutgers, test that you have configured your device correctly by attempting to connect to the eduroam network while on the Rutgers campus with your NetID in the form of NetID@rutgers.edu and your NetID password.
•	If you are having trouble configuring your device for eduroam or connecting to eduroam while traveling to another institution, contact your local computing Help Desk. Note that the IT personnel at the institution you are visiting will not be able to assist you with authentication issues that may prevent you from accessing eduroam.
Security reminders while traveling
•	When visiting other institutions, members of the Rutgers community must adhere to the guidelines outlined in the Rutgers Acceptable Use Policy.
•	Use Rutgers VPN on your laptop, smartphone, or tablet to create an encrypted connection to University resources.
•	Install antivirus software on your devices.
•	Assume that any networks or devices other than your own are insecure. Remember that eduroam will never show a webpage asking for your username and/or password. This is a sign that someone is attempting to hijack your password – do not use any network that requests this information.
Information to complete a manual installation
See the manual configuration settings for eduroam.
For Eduroam Frequently Asked Questions, please visit Eduroam's website.

title: and Collaboration Services Daily Email Sending Limits
body:
Starting December 11, 2024, the daily sending limit for individual user accounts in both Rutgers Connect and ScarletMail will be set to 1,000 messages per person, irrespective of the email's destination. The number of emails sent daily is calculated based on a rolling 24-hour period, not a calendar day, where each recipient counts as one email towards the limit. On ScarletMail, there is an additional restriction that the total number of recipients in the To, CC, and BCC fields is limited to 500 per email.  
The daily limit only applies to an individual's account and does not apply to emails sent from a distribution list or 365 Group. Additionally, when sending an email to a distribution list address with multiple recipients, it will only count as one email towards the daily sending limit. 
When sending an email from a shared mailbox, you must open the shared mailbox directly, since simply changing the "From" address while in your personal email account still counts against your daily limit. Follow the instructions on how to open the shared mailbox in a separate browser window and how to send emails from the shared mailbox.
This adjustment is necessary due to recent increases in email attacks. By lowering the sending limits and reducing the number of recipients per email, Rutgers can better protect against abuse and support a secure environment. 
Approved bulk mailer services like Rutgers Automated Mass-Mailing Service (RAMS) and Mailman will not be affected and should be utilized for individuals wanting to email a large audience. Contact your Departmental IT Support for additional guidance on your bulk emailing options.

title: and Collaboration Services Email accounts exceeding daily send limit (for Delegated Administrators)
body:
Starting December 11, 2024, the daily sending limit for individual user accounts in both Rutgers Connect and ScarletMail will be set to 1,000 messages per person, irrespective of the email's destination.
On ScarletMail, there is an additional restriction that the total number of recipients in the To, CC, and BCC fields is limited to 500 per email. 
The daily limit only applies to an individual's account and does not apply to emails sent from a distribution list or 365 Group. In addition, when sending an email to a distribution list address with multiple people on the list, it will only count as one email towards the daily sending limit. 
When sending email from a shared mailbox, you must open the shared mailbox directly, since simply changing the "From" address while in your personal email account still counts against your daily limit. Follow the instructions on how to open and send mail from the shared mailbox in a separate browser window.
Why an account is blocked
The limit will be imposed on user accounts only. Occasionally, a shared account may trigger a block and is handled as noted below. An account can be blocked from sending emails for any of the following reasons:
•	Sending any number of emails to 1,000 different user accounts (both internal and external accounts)
•	Forwarding any number of emails to 1,000 different user accounts (both internal and external accounts)
•	Adding over 500 users to the To/CC/BCC fields of an email several times on ScarletMail
The number of emails sent daily is calculated based on a rolling 24-hour period, not a calendar day, where each recipient counts as one email towards the limit. 
When it is detected that any of the limits have been met, the account is automatically blocked, and an incident is created in ServiceNow for Connect Support. 
User notification of a block
Users will see one of the following messages when sending an email after their account has been blocked. 
Rutgers Connect
"This message can't be sent because you've reached your daily limit for message recipients."
ScarletMail
"You have reached a limit for sending email."
"You reached a Gmail sending limit."
"You exceeded the maximum recipients."
Resolving blocks
Rutgers Connect
For any block that occurs for a Connect account, an Incident is automatically created in ServiceNow for Connect Support to review. They then review the account to confirm it is not compromised and determine the activity that generated the block before taking the following steps.
If they are legitimate emails, internal to Rutgers, and it is a shared account
•	The shared account is unblocked.
•	It is added to an exceptions list to prevent any recurring blocks. The exception list is still subject to hard limits imposed by Microsoft. There is a 2,500 limit on emails sent to external addresses, per rolling 24 hours. 
•	The appropriate Delegated Admins are notified of this occurrence.
If they are legitimate emails, internal to Rutgers, and it is a user account
•	The appropriate Delegated Admins are notified of this occurrence and informed of the various options/strategies to mitigate the cause of the block. 
•	The block is left in place until the Delegated Admins indicate they are working with the user or until 24 hours have passed. 
If they are legitimate emails and include external (non-RU) contacts
•	Regardless of account type, the appropriate Delegated Admins are notified of this occurrence and informed of the various options/strategies to mitigate the cause of the block. 
•	The block is left in place until the Delegated Admins indicate they are working with the user or until 24 hours have passed.
If the logs do not indicate the triggering behavior
•	The account is unblocked.
•	The appropriate Delegated Admins are notified of this occurrence and asked to contact the user.
All correspondence with the Delegated Admins is copied to the Incident, and it is resolved when merited or if 24 hours have passed and a block is no longer in place.
ScarletMail
Delegated Administrators are not typically available on the ScarletMail platform.
In these situations, the OIT Help Desk and ScarletMail service owners will evaluate the issue and work with the user or resolve the incident as appropriate

title: and Collaboration Services Shared storage space options
body:
For groups or departments that want a shared space to store files that is not tied directly to one individual, the following options are available. 
Microsoft Teams – Departmental creation 
Microsoft Teams lets you choose a group of people with whom you wish to collaborate and easily set up a collection of resources for them to share. Items in the group's resources (Calendar, OneDrive, OneNote) will automatically be shared with all of the members of the group. To learn more about the features available, visit the Microsoft Teams webpage on the Rutgers IT website.  
Eligibility 
Departments can request a team by contacting your Rutgers Connect Delegated Administrator. 
Storage limits 
Microsoft Teams starts with 1TB of SharePoint storage. If you need additional space, please contact your Rutgers Connect Delegated Administrator. 
How to use a departmental Microsoft Team account  
If you would like a Microsoft Teams departmental account, please contact your Rutgers Connect Delegated Administrator to request that one be created for you. To learn more on the features available, see the article on Getting started with Microsoft Teams or browse Microsoft’s Teams support page for more detailed information. 
Microsoft Teams – Self-creation 
A self-created Microsoft Teams account is a limited version of Microsoft Teams that may be created without the involvement of a Rutgers Connect Delegated Administrator. Some differences are noted below. 
•	There is no unified group mailbox to view in Rutgers Connect. You can only send mail to specific channels within the team itself. 
•	Teams are restricted to the @teams.rutgers.edu domain and have a stricter naming policy.  
•	Owners can update or change the name of their Team in the Teams’ settings. 
•	After 400 days of inactivity, the Team owner(s) will receive an email notification from Microsoft stating that their Team will expire unless action is taken. The notice for Teams without an active owner, or no owner, will be sent to help@oit.rutgers.edu. 
•	The maximum available storage is 1TB. 
Eligibility 
Anyone with a Rutgers Connect account can create a team via the Teams application.  
Storage limits 
Microsoft Teams starts with 1TB of SharePoint storage. 
How to use a self-created Teams account 
Visit the Creating a Team article or Microsoft Teams support page for more information. 
Box departmental accounts 
A departmental account, also known as a shared account, is an account controlled by Rutgers IT delegated administrators who create sub-level folder shares from within that account to provide to their various user populations. Generally, only the delegated administrators for the domain have access to that top level. OIT considers a shared account to be the collective total resource, not the individual folders that are shared out to various departments.  
Eligibility 
Shared Box accounts are available to departments and their respective users. For a shared account, reach out to your Rutgers IT delegated administrator. 
Storage limits 
Shared Box accounts have a minimum storage limit of 25 TB. Shared accounts are considered the collective total resource of the account, not the individual folders that are shared with various departments.  
How to use Box 
To learn more, visit the getting started with Box article.   
ScarletMail Groups 
Shared storage on ScarletMail is not currently available at Rutgers. You can instead create a Google Group, which can include a collaborative Inbox that multiple people can access. However, files in a Google Group are owned by an individual and count against their ScarletMail storage limit.  
Eligibility 
ScarletMail accounts are available to Faculty, Staff, Students, Retirees, Professor Emeritus, and Guests. 
Storage limits 
When you share a file with a Google Group, it utilizes the individual file owner's storage. No additional shared storage space is provided. 
How to use Groups 
For more information on the features available, visit the article on what is a Google Group.  
For instructions on creating and using a Group, visit Google's Support guide on Groups.

title: Generative AI Tools Getting Started with ChatGPT
body:
ChatGPT is an AI-powered conversational assistant developed by OpenAI that can help with writing, research, brainstorming, coding, data analysis, and more. Rutgers University offers ChatGPT Edu subscriptions through the University Software Portal, providing faculty, staff, and students with an enterprise-grade version of ChatGPT that includes enhanced data protections.
ChatGPT Edu is specifically designed for higher education institutions and ensures that your conversations and data are not used to train OpenAI’s models. This makes it a safer option for university-related work compared to using a free personal ChatGPT account.
Table of Contents
•	Appropriate Use
•	Safety and Data Protection 
o	Use Your Rutgers Account
o	What You Should Know
o	Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
•	How to Get Started
•	Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Other Free AI Tools at Rutgers
•	Links
Appropriate Use
ChatGPT can be a valuable tool when used responsibly in an academic and professional setting. Common use cases include:
•	Writing assistance - Drafting, editing, and proofreading emails, reports, proposals, and other documents.
•	Research support - Summarizing articles, generating literature review outlines, and exploring topics.
•	Teaching and learning - Creating lesson plans, generating practice problems, explaining complex concepts, and providing feedback on student work.
•	Brainstorming - Generating ideas for projects, presentations, grant proposals, and creative assignments.
•	Coding help - Writing, debugging, and explaining code across a variety of programming languages.
•	Data analysis - Interpreting data sets, generating charts, and summarizing findings.
•	Administrative tasks - Drafting communications, creating agendas, and organizing information.
Always review AI-generated content for accuracy before using it in any official capacity. ChatGPT can produce plausible-sounding but incorrect information (often called “hallucinations”), so human oversight remains essential.
Safety and Data Protection
Use Your Rutgers Account
When you access ChatGPT through a Rutgers ChatGPT Edu subscription, your data is protected by OpenAI’s enterprise-level data handling agreements with the university. Your conversations and data are not used to train OpenAI’s models. This protection does not apply when using a free personal ChatGPT account.
What You Should Know
•	Do not enter protected health information (PHI), Social Security numbers, or other highly sensitive data into ChatGPT, even with a Rutgers subscription.
•	Do not rely on ChatGPT for critical decisions without verifying the information through authoritative sources.
•	Be aware of academic integrity policies. Students should consult their instructors and course syllabi regarding the acceptable use of AI tools in coursework.
•	ChatGPT may not always be accurate. It can generate incorrect facts, fabricated citations, and flawed reasoning. Always verify important information.
Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
Personal vs University Accounts
Feature	Personal (Free) Account	Rutgers ChatGPT Edu
Data used for model training	Yes	No
Enterprise data protections	No	Yes
Institutional support	No	Yes
Using the Rutgers-provided subscription is strongly recommended for any university-related work.
How to Get Started
1.	Visit the University Software Portal and search for ChatGPT Edu.
2.	Purchase a subscription. ChatGPT Edu subscriptions start at $10 per month. Faculty and staff can purchase subscriptions for themselves or for members of their department.
3.	Log in to ChatGPT using your Rutgers credentials (your netid@rutgers.edu address).
4.	Start a conversation by typing a question or prompt in the message box.
Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Be specific with your prompts. Instead of asking “Tell me about climate change,” try “Summarize the three most significant effects of climate change on coastal ecosystems in the northeastern United States, citing recent research.”
•	Provide context. Let ChatGPT know your role, audience, and purpose. For example: “I’m a professor preparing a lecture for undergraduate biology students. Help me explain CRISPR gene editing in simple terms.”
•	Iterate on responses. If the first response isn’t quite right, ask ChatGPT to refine, expand, or adjust its answer.
•	Use system instructions. You can set custom instructions in your ChatGPT settings to tailor responses to your needs across all conversations.
Other Free AI Tools at Rutgers
Before subscribing to ChatGPT Edu, consider that Rutgers also provides free access to other AI tools, including Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. The Office of Information Technology recommends exploring these free alternatives unless your unit has an immediate need for ChatGPT Edu.

title: Generative AI Tools Getting Started with Google Gemini
body:
Google Gemini is an AI-powered assistant developed by Google, available to all Rutgers faculty, staff, and students at no cost through their ScarletApps (Google Workspace for Education) accounts. All Rutgers faculty, staff, and student ScarletApps accounts have access to the Gemini app, available via web, desktop, or mobile clients. With an optional, free, upgrade to Google Workspace for Education Plus, Gemini can help with writing, research, brainstorming, summarization, coding, and creative tasks directly within the Google tools you already use.
When you sign in with your Rutgers ScarletApps account, Gemini operates under Google Workspace for Education’s enterprise data protections. This means your conversations and data are not used to train Google’s AI models, making it a safer choice for university-related work than a personal Google account.
Table of Contents
•	Appropriate Use
•	Safety and Data Protection 
o	Use Your Rutgers ScarletApps Account
o	What You Should Know
o	Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
•	Known Limitations
•	How to Get Started
•	Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Upgrade to Google AI Pro
•	API Access
•	Links
Appropriate Use
Gemini is a versatile tool that can support a wide range of academic and professional tasks:
•	Writing and editing - Draft emails, reports, and documents; get suggestions for improving clarity and tone.
•	Research and summarization - Quickly summarize long documents, articles, or web pages. Use Deep Research to have Gemini conduct a web search on your behalf.
•	Brainstorming - Generate ideas for projects, presentations, lesson plans, and assignments.
•	Google Workspace integration - Use Google Workspace for Education Plus to directly access Gemini within Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, and more for context-aware assistance.
•	Coding assistance - Write, debug, explain, and preview the output of code in multiple programming or markup languages, including TeX.
•	Learning and tutoring - Break down complex topics, create study guides, and generate practice questions.
•	Media generation - Generate videos, music, and audio overviews. With Google Workspace for Education Plus, produce studio-quality AI-generated voiceovers.
•	Media understanding - Upload images or videos for Gemini to analyze, describe, or discuss.
As with all AI tools, always review Gemini’s output for accuracy. AI-generated content can contain errors, fabricated information, or biased perspectives.
Safety and Data Protection
Use Your Rutgers ScarletApps Account
When you access Gemini through your Rutgers ScarletApps account, your conversations are protected by Google Workspace for Education’s enterprise data agreements. Your data is not used to train Google’s AI models. This protection does not apply when using a personal Gmail account.
What You Should Know
•	Do not enter protected health information (PHI), Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, or other highly sensitive data into Gemini.
•	Do not rely on Gemini for critical decisions without verifying the information through authoritative sources.
•	Be aware of academic integrity policies. Students should check with their instructors about the acceptable use of AI tools in coursework.
•	Gemini may produce inaccurate information. Always fact-check important claims, especially citations and statistics.
Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
Personal vs University Accounts
Feature	Personal Google Account	Rutgers ScarletApps Account
Data used for model training	Yes	No
Enterprise data protections	No	Yes
Google Workspace integration	Limited	Full
Institutional compliance	No	Yes
Always use your Rutgers ScarletApps account for university-related work.
Known Limitations
There are two known limitations with Gemini on Google Workspace for Education accounts that are important to be aware of:
•	Gems are currently disabled. Rutgers has turned off the Gems feature (custom Gemini personas) for security reasons. Once Google addresses these security concerns, Gems will be enabled, and this documentation will be updated accordingly.
•	Chat history cannot be deleted. The inability to delete individual chat conversations is a Google limitation with Gemini on Workspace for Education accounts. Google is working on resolving this issue, and this documentation will be updated once a fix is available.
How to Get Started
1.	Go to Gemini.
2.	Sign in with your Rutgers ScarletApps account (your netid@scarletmail.rutgers.edu address). If you are currently signed into a personal Google account, switch to your Rutgers account first.
3.	Start a conversation by typing a question or prompt in the message box.
4.	Try Gemini's Tools - Under the Tools dropdown, choose an option such as Canvas (interactive document/code generation) or Guided Learning (has Gemini attempt to lead you to learning the answer, instead of instantly giving you the answer).
Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Be clear and specific. Provide enough detail in your prompts for Gemini to understand what you need. For example: “Summarize this 10-page research paper on renewable energy policy into 5 bullet points suitable for a departmental briefing.”
•	Provide context about your role and audience. For example: “I’m a graduate teaching assistant. Help me create a rubric for evaluating undergraduate research proposals.”
•	Use follow-up prompts. Continue the conversation to refine responses. Ask Gemini to expand on a point, change the tone, or reformat the output.
•	Upload files for analysis. You can upload documents, images, and other files for Gemini to analyze and discuss.
•	Leverage Workspace integration. Use the free upgrade to Google Workspace for Education Plus to access the Gemini side panel in Google Docs and other Google document editors. For example, ask the side panel to help you fix a bug in your Google Sheets =FORMULA syntax.
Upgrade to Google AI Pro
For users who need more advanced capabilities, Rutgers offers Google AI Pro for Education subscriptions through the University Software Portal. Purchasers enjoy higher usage limits, access to premium AI models, and enhanced video generation and foreign language capabilities. Faculty and staff can purchase subscriptions for themselves or assign them to others.
Google maintains a regularly updated PDF that describes the current differences between Fundamentals (the base ScarletApps account), Google Workspace for Education Plus, and Google AI Pro for Education. These differences are not part of Rutgers' contract, and are subject to change without notice.
API Access
Neither the free Gemini license nor the AI Pro for Education subscription includes access to the Gemini API. For programmatic access to Google's AI models, please contact OIT's Cloud Services team.

title: Generative AI Tools Getting Started with Google NotebookLM
body:
Google NotebookLM is a free AI-powered research and note-taking tool that helps you understand, summarize, and interact with your own collection of public and private source materials. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, NotebookLM is grounded in the sources you provide - it analyzes your uploaded materials (PDFs, Google Docs, web links, YouTube videos, and more) and generates responses based specifically on that content. This makes it especially useful in academic settings where accuracy and source attribution matter.
NotebookLM is available to all Rutgers faculty, staff, and students at no cost through their ScarletApps (Google Workspace for Education) accounts.
Table of Contents
•	Appropriate Use 
o	For Faculty
o	For Students
o	For Staff
•	Safety and Data Protection 
o	Use Your Rutgers ScarletApps Account
o	What You Should Know
o	Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
•	How to Get Started
•	Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Upgrade to NotebookLM Plus or NotebookLM Pro
•	Links
Appropriate Use
NotebookLM is particularly well-suited for tasks that involve working with specific source materials or for sharing AI technology with others, such as a project team or a study group. Here are some valuable use cases:
For Faculty
•	Course preparation - Upload syllabi, textbooks, and research papers to quickly generate lecture summaries, discussion questions, and study guides.
•	Research synthesis - Load multiple papers into a notebook to identify common themes, contradictions, and gaps across the literature.
•	Grading and feedback - Upload rubrics and student work samples to help draft consistent, detailed feedback.
•	Grant writing - Organize research notes, prior publications, and funding guidelines in a notebook to help draft proposal sections.
•	Meeting preparation - Upload agendas, prior meeting notes, and related documents to quickly get up to speed.
•	Chat-only notebook sharing - Prepare a set of vetted source materials for your students. Then, share the notebook as "chat-only," ensuring that students do not influence the source material used by other students.
For Students
•	Study and review - Upload class notes, slides, and readings to generate summaries, flashcards, and practice questions.
•	Research projects - Load research sources into a notebook and ask questions to identify key arguments, compare perspectives, and find relevant quotes with citations.
•	Paper writing - Upload your draft along with your sources to check whether your arguments are well-supported and identify areas that need more evidence.
•	Exam preparation - Create notebooks organized by topic or course module and use the Q&A feature to test your understanding. Flashcards, quizzes, mind maps, and more are supported.
•	Multimedia overviews - Generate audio or video summaries of your sources to review material on the go, similar to listening to a podcast about your own notes.
For Staff
•	Policy review - Upload policy documents, guidelines, and procedures to quickly find answers to specific questions.
•	Report generation - Load data reports and meeting notes to help draft executive summaries and briefings.
•	Training materials - Upload reference documents to create FAQ guides and training outlines for new team members.
As with all AI tools, always verify NotebookLM’s output against your original sources. While NotebookLM is grounded in your uploaded materials, it can still occasionally misinterpret or oversimplify complex content.
Safety and Data Protection
Use Your Rutgers ScarletApps Account
When you access NotebookLM through your Rutgers ScarletApps account, your data is protected by Google Workspace for Education’s enterprise data agreements. Your uploaded documents and conversations are not used to train Google’s AI models. This protection does not apply when using a personal Google account.
What You Should Know
•	Do not upload protected health information (PHI), Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, or other highly sensitive data to NotebookLM.
•	NotebookLM responses are only as good as the sources you use. If your uploaded materials contain errors, NotebookLM’s responses may reflect those errors.
•	Be aware of academic integrity policies. Students should consult their instructors about the acceptable use of AI tools for coursework. NotebookLM is a research aid, not a substitute for original analysis and critical thinking.
•	Verify citations and quotes. While NotebookLM provides source references, always check the original documents to ensure accuracy.
Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
Personal vs University Accounts
Feature	Personal Google Account	Rutgers ScarletApps Account
Data used for model training	May be used	No
Enterprise data protections	No	Yes
Institutional compliance	No	Yes
Always use your Rutgers ScarletApps account for university-related work.
How to Get Started
1.	Go to NotebookLM.
2.	Sign in with your Rutgers ScarletApps account (your netid@scarletmail.rutgers.edu address). If you are currently signed into a personal Google account, switch to your Rutgers account first.
3.	Create a new notebook by clicking the “New Notebook” button.
4.	Add sources by uploading PDFs, linking to Google Docs, pasting website URLs, adding YouTube videos, or pasting text directly.
5.	Start asking questions about your sources in the chat panel. NotebookLM will respond based on the content you provided and cite the specific sources it used.
Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Be intentional about your sources. NotebookLM works best when your uploaded materials are relevant and focused. A notebook with 5-10 well-chosen sources will produce better results than one with 50 loosely related documents.
•	Use the notebook guide. After uploading sources, check the automatically generated notebook guide for an overview of your materials and suggested questions.
•	Ask specific questions. Instead of “What is this about?”, try “What are the three main arguments in the Smith 2024 paper regarding climate policy?”
•	Generate audio overviews. Use the Audio Overview feature to create a podcast-style summary of your sources - great for reviewing material during a commute.
•	Organize by project or course. Create separate notebooks for each course, research project, or work initiative to keep your materials organized.
•	Pin important notes. Save useful AI-generated summaries and responses as notes within your notebook for easy reference later.
Upgrade to NotebookLM Plus or NotebookLM Pro
For users who need more advanced capabilities, Rutgers offers Google Workspace for Education Plus (centrally funded by Rutgers OIT; no cost to users) and Google AI Pro for Education (paid) subscriptions through the University Software Portal. Search for Workspace Plus or AI Pro if you feel you need higher usage limits or access to premium AI models. Faculty and staff can purchase subscriptions for themselves or assign them to others.

title: Generative AI Tools Getting Started with Microsoft Copilot
body:
Microsoft Copilot is an AI-powered assistant available to all Rutgers faculty, staff, and students at no cost when accessed using your Rutgers Connect account. Copilot can help with writing, summarizing documents, answering questions, generating images, drafting emails, writing code, and more. When you sign in with your Rutgers credentials, your data is protected by Microsoft’s enterprise data handling agreements and is not used to train Copilot’s foundation models.
Rutgers provides Copilot access as part of the university’s existing Microsoft licensing. There is also a separate, paid Microsoft 365 Copilot product that offers deeper integration with Microsoft 365 applications like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Teams.
Table of Contents

Appropriate Use
Microsoft Copilot is a versatile AI assistant suitable for a wide range of academic and professional tasks:
•	Writing and editing - Draft, proofread, and refine emails, reports, proposals, and other documents.
•	Research and summarization - Summarize articles, web pages, and documents; get quick answers to factual questions.
•	Brainstorming - Generate ideas for projects, presentations, lesson plans, and creative work.
•	Image generation - Create original images from text descriptions using DALL-E integration.
•	Coding assistance - Write, explain, and debug code in multiple programming languages.
•	Data analysis - Help interpret data, create formulas, and explain statistical concepts.
•	Presentation preparation - Outline presentations, suggest talking points, and help organize content.
As with all AI tools, always review Copilot’s output for accuracy. AI-generated content can contain errors, outdated information, or biased perspectives.
Safety and Data Protection
Use Your Rutgers Account
When you access Copilot by signing in with your Rutgers email and NetID password, your data is protected by Microsoft’s enterprise-level privacy and security commitments. Your data is not used to train Copilot’s foundation models. This protection does not apply when using Copilot with a personal Microsoft account.
What You Should Know
•	When possible, avoid entering protected health information (PHI), Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, or other highly sensitive data into Copilot.
•	Do not rely on Copilot for critical decisions without verifying the information through authoritative sources.
•	Be aware of academic integrity policies. Students should consult their instructors about the acceptable use of AI tools in coursework.
•	Copilot may produce inaccurate information. Always fact-check important claims, especially citations, statistics, and technical details.
Personal Accounts vs. University Accounts
Personal vs Rutgers Accounts
Feature	Personal Microsoft Account	Rutgers Account
Data used for model training	May be used	No
Enterprise data protections	No	Yes
Encryption and privacy safeguards	Basic	Enterprise-grade
Institutional compliance	No	Yes
Always use your Rutgers account for university-related work.
Copilot vs. Microsoft 365 Copilot
Rutgers provides two levels of Copilot access. Here is a high-level overview of the differences:
Copilot (Included with your Rutgers Connect Account)
This is the AI chatbot available to everyone at Rutgers at no additional cost. It provides a conversational AI assistant that can answer questions, help with writing, generate images, and assist with coding. However, the Copilot chatbot does not include integrations with other Microsoft 365 tools like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, or Teams.
Microsoft 365 Copilot (Paid Add-On)
Microsoft 365 Copilot is a paid subscription that embeds AI assistance directly into Microsoft 365 applications. It can draft documents in Word, create presentations in PowerPoint, analyze data in Excel, summarize email threads in Outlook, and assist during meetings in Teams. This deeper integration allows Copilot to work with your existing files and organizational data.
For detailed information about Microsoft 365 Copilot features, licensing, and pricing, visit the University Software Portal and search for Microsoft 365 Copilot. Faculty and staff can purchase subscriptions for themselves or assign them to others.
How to Get Started
1.	Go to Microsoft Copilot.
2.	Sign in with your Rutgers email and NetID password. This ensures your data is protected under the university’s enterprise agreement.
3.	Start a conversation by typing a question or prompt in the message box.
4.	Try different types of tasks - Ask Copilot to write an email, summarize a topic, generate an image, help with code, or answer a question.
Tips for Getting Better Results
•	Be specific with your prompts. Instead of “Write an email,” try “Write a professional email to my department announcing a schedule change for next week’s seminar, keeping the tone friendly and concise.”
•	Provide context. Let Copilot know your role and audience. For example: “I’m an academic advisor. Help me draft a message to students about course registration deadlines.”
•	Iterate on responses. If the first response isn’t what you need, ask Copilot to adjust. You can say things like “Make it shorter,” “Use a more formal tone,” or “Add more detail about the second point.”
•	Use follow-up questions. Continue the conversation to dive deeper into a topic or refine the output.
•	Try image generation. Describe an image you’d like to create, and Copilot will generate it using DALL-E. This can be useful for presentations, teaching materials, or creative projects.

title: FAQ
body:
Table of Contents
•	When will I lose the ability to log in to ArcGIS?
•	What should I do before losing access to ArcGIS Online?
•	What happens to my content if I do nothing?
•	What does the Esri Education Institution License allow?
•	Can I work on Rutgers projects after leaving?
•	Can I access my content after leaving Rutgers?
•	How do I transfer ownership to another Rutgers user?
•	How do I obtain and transfer content to an ArcGIS for Personal Use subscription?
When will I lose the ability to log in to ArcGIS?
Your access to ArcGIS Online is tied to your role at Rutgers University. If you are an active student, staff, faculty, or sponsored affiliate, your Rutgers account remains authorized. After graduating or leaving, you will lose login access, but your content will not be deleted immediately. Students not enrolled over Spring/Summer but returning in the Fall retain access as usual. 
What should I do before losing access to ArcGIS Online?
To maintain access to your content (Web Maps, StoryMaps, etc.), transfer it from your Rutgers account to another ArcGIS Online location. Options include:
•	Transfer to another Rutgers user: If your content is needed by others at Rutgers, transfer ownership to them. See the ESRI ArcGIS Transfer Request.
•	Transfer to an ArcGIS for Personal Use subscription: This paid option ($100/year) lets you continue working on your content and access Esri training materials. More information can be found on the ArcGIS for Personal Use website.
•	Delete your content: Remove anything you no longer need. Content will eventually be deleted after you leave.
If you need help determining what to do with your content, assistance with the various transfer options, or have other questions about ArcGIS, contact us at software@rutgers.edu. 
What happens to my content if I do nothing?
Content is not deleted immediately after you leave Rutgers. Content will be deleted only if the owner has not logged in for 3 years, and no one has viewed the content in 3 years.
What does the Esri Education Institution License allow?
Rutgers’ license covers unlimited use for university-related academic purposes (teaching and research). For details, see the general terms and Rubric for Permitted Uses. For licensing questions, contact software@rutgers.edu.
Can I work on Rutgers projects after leaving?
Ask your Rutgers collaborator to sponsor you for a Guest NetID. You may only use ArcGIS as a Sponsored Affiliate for Rutgers projects. 
Can I access my content after leaving Rutgers?
•	Publicly shared content remains accessible to everyone.
•	Content shared privately or with a group is not accessible after you lose login access.
•	Group members can still access content shared with the group, as long as they remain active at Rutgers. 
How do I transfer ownership to another Rutgers user?
See the ESRI ArcGIS Transfer Request.
How do I obtain and transfer content to an ArcGIS for Personal Use subscription?
Visit the ArcGIS for Personal Use website. Most content can be transferred using ArcGIS Online Assistant, except StoryMaps. For StoryMaps, contact software@rutgers.edu.

title: Getting started with Grammarly for Education
body:
Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that checks for spelling, grammar, and punctuation errors. It offers plagiarism-detection services and advanced writing suggestions to improve clarity, vocabulary, style, and tone.
Features
Improve your communication in and out of the classroom with Grammarly’s suite of offerings, including:
•	Grammar and spelling suggestions: Check for grammatical and spelling errors in real-time.
•	Tone detection: Access enhanced tone and vocabulary recommendations.
•	Citations: Receive suggestions for citation formatting and management.
•	Plagiarism detection: Check against billions of pages and academic papers to ensure you don’t submit unoriginal writing.
•	Integrations: Available across devices as a standalone application or add-on extension for browsers. 
Getting Started
Accessing your account
Faculty, staff, and students can activate their Rutgers Grammarly for Education account or convert an existing personal account by following the guide on how to activate Grammarly.
After your account has been activated, you can access it by logging into the Rutgers Grammarly link or entering your netid@rutgers.edu email address on the Grammarly website. 
User Guide
Visit Grammarly's User Guide for more information on the available features and settings. Note that not all features in this guide may be available. 
Installing Grammarly
You can download the desktop/mobile applications or the browser extension by logging in to the Grammarly Apps page on the device you want to install it on. The website will automatically detect the Operating System (OS) and browser you are using. Visit the Grammarly Support page for detailed instructions on installing.

title: for Education account audits
body:
Who can have a Grammarly for Education account?
According to Office of Information Technology guidelines, only the following classes of people are eligible to have Grammarly for Education accounts:
•	On-boarded (current and future) employees of Rutgers University
•	Current students
•	Professor Emeritus
•	Guests: individuals conducting University business and directly associated with the University but are not officially on the University's payroll. Examples of guests include visiting professors/scholars, members of auxiliary groups, and others working on University business or affiliated with the University.
The following groups of people are not automatically eligible for Grammarly for Education accounts:
•	Former employees (including teaching/graduate assistants who may still be students but are not actively working for Rutgers)
•	Alumni
•	Retirees
How can I keep my Grammarly for Education account?
We determine which accounts should be closed by comparing Grammarly for Education accounts with the active roles (e.g. Faculty or Staff) of NetIDs listed in the University’s OpenRegistry (OR) service, which is used as the basis for the Rutgers Online Directory. The OR may have some information that needs correction.
Current Employees
You may not be listed in the OR as a current employee. To check this, go to the Search for People tool and search for your name. Review each result if you get more than one. Contact your department’s Human Resources person if your name does not appear.
When your entry appears, review the information there. If it is incorrect, contact the person in your department’s Human Resources.
Students
If you are a current student, first verify your status in OR. To check this, go to the Search for People tool and search for your name. Review each result if you get more than one. If your name does not appear, please inquire about your registration via One Stop.
When your entry appears, review the information there. If it is incorrect, please inquire about your registration via One Stop.
Guests
If you are affiliated with Rutgers but not actually employed by Rutgers, you may request a guest account. Have a sponsor at the department you are working with go to the Guest Account site, and submit a request for you, which will be sent to our Accounts Office for processing.
Every year, you must renew your guest account. You will be notified when it's time to renew your account (30 days prior to its expiration).
Your Rutgers Connect Delegated Administrator can assist your sponsor in submitting a Guest Account request and, if necessary, creating your account.
What should I do before the account is closed?
Before losing your Grammarly account, it is recommended that you download any files you may have saved in the Grammarly Editor.
What is the typical account audit timeline?
When it is determined that you no longer have an active role at the University that entitles you to a Grammarly account, your account will be locked for 30 days. During this time, use of your account will be unavailable. However, you may not be logged out immediately, and saved cookies on your device may allow limited Grammarly functionality for a short time. 
After 30 days, your account and any associated data are deleted. 
For further assistance
If you have any questions about the above, contact the OIT Help Desk.

title: NetID Guest NetIDs and Accounts
body:
Guest accounts are intended to support the activities of Rutgers University. Guests are expected to use their Rutgers accounts only in support of their work with Rutgers, as described in their guest account application. More detailed policies are contained in the Guest Account Policies section of the Computing Policies page. All guests and their sponsors are responsible for abiding by the policies described on that page, including specifically the Acceptable Use Policy and Guest Policy.
Guest Accounts For Faculty and Staff
A full-time Rutgers faculty or staff member can request a guest account. This individual will be considered the University sponsor and will be expected to maintain contact with the guest.
Annual renewal notifications will be addressed to the sponsor and the guest.
To request a guest account, the sponsoring department should complete the online form located on the Guest Request System. 
Guest Accounts for Faculty/Staff Retirement
Retired Rutgers employees who have served the university for a minimum of 10 years can apply for retention of their ScarletMail accounts following retirement.
To do so, they must contact the Rutgers Retired Faculty and Staff Center, University Human Resources located at ASB II, 57 US Highway 1, New Brunswick, NJ 08901-8554, by phone (848) 932-3580 or email retireecenter@hr.rutgers.edu.
The retiree will then be directed to the Guest Request System to submit a guest request. Once the request has been approved, the retiree's ScarletMail account will be subject to all guest account regulations.
An annual audit of ScarletMail accounts will be conducted. The retiree should reply to the audit email message sent out to maintain his/her ScarletMail account. If no reply is received by the due date, the account will be closed during the next regularly scheduled account closing time.
Changing the Sponsor of a Guest
If the sponsor needs to be changed for a guest for any reason, such as the current sponsor leaving the University, submit a new guest request with the new sponsor and note in the request that it is to change the sponsor. 
Contact Information
For assistance, please contact the OIT Help Desk at: 833-OIT-HELP (648-4357) or email help@oit.rutgers.edu.

title: FAQs How can I enable/disable Speaker Track on Touch 10?
body:
Speaker Track allows the camera to follow whoever is speaking. Speaker Track can be enabled/disabled through the Touch 10 system.
1.	Open the call controls, or at any time, open the control panel and tap the Camera button.
2.	Choose a camera mode. 
o	Group: The camera will adjust to show everyone.
o	Frames: The camera will zoom and show people individually or in smaller groups.
o	Speaker: The camera will follow the person speaking. The maximum distance for speaker tracking to work is 7.5 meters.
3.	Tap outside the camera options screen to exit.
More information about this can be found in the Touch 10 user manual.

title: FAQs How can I share a presentation from another device to the Touch 10?
body:
A presentation can be shared from another device using the Multi-Connector or via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth using Proximity.
Multi-Connector set up
1.	Plug the Multi-Connector into your laptop.
2.	On the Cisco Touch 10 unit, there will be two options: 
o	Local Preview: will only be visible in your room, allowing you to see what you will be sharing before actually doing so.
o	Share in Call: will share your screen with all call recipients.
Proximity set up
To use Proximity, the Cisco Telepresence Unit must have Proximity enabled. The user should speak with their local IT for this.
Proximity is available for download from the Cisco website, the App Store, or the Google Play Store.
Proximity on Desktop
1.	After downloading and installing the Proximity, launch the application.
2.	The application will search the area for proximity-enabled Cisco Touch Units.
3.	Once a system is found, the PC will be automatically connected.
4.	Once connected, there will be two options: Share Screen or Make a Call.
5.	When connected, the PC effectively works as the Touch 10 unit.
Proximity on Mobile Device
1.	From the App Store or Google Play Store, download the Proximity app.
2.	Open the Proximity app.
3.	The Proximity app will begin searching for a Proximity-enabled Cisco Touch Unit.
4.	Once connected to a CTU, the user can Share Screen or Make a Call.
For more information, visit Cisco's PDF Handbook on Cisco TelePresence User Guide Systems Using Touch 10.

title: FAQ Can KACE perform security patches and upgrade applications to new versions?
body:
Quest works with a list of vendors to obtain the most up to date patches for both applications and operating systems. Quest tests each patch before making them available for download on the KACE appliance. Each organization can configure which patches they wish to subscribe to, as well as the type of patches (critical, recommended, and optional).
Software updates to new versions can be accomplished via the Software Distribution feature. This feature allows the installation of upgrades and new applications remotely to client systems in multiple locations.

title: FAQ
body:
"Can patching be configured to exclude systems, which may be sensitive to patching?"
The Patch Management feature allows the unit computing staff to restrict the distribution to specific systems or groups of systems. This allows an individual system or group of systems to be excluded from receiving patches.

title: FAQ How can I obtain a KACE Organization for my department?
body:
To request a KACE organization, please fill out the KACE New ORG Request form. 
If you have any questions, please contact KACE_support@oit.rutgers.edu.

title: FAQ How does KACE work?
body:
A small application will be installed on the client systems, the KACE Amp Agent. This agent periodically scans the system to collect inventory data, which is then sent back to the appliance. This agent is required to perform the following tasks.
•	Software Distribution
•	Software Metering
•	Scripting
•	Patching
Alternatively, a client system can be inventoried via the Agentless Inventory feature. This might be used on a mission critical server or a system where an agent does not exist. The agentless inventory feature can also track additional devices, such as Dell projectors and printers. Client systems utilizing Agentless Inventory will be sent a command from the KACE system periodically to collect data.

title: FAQ How is Rutgers using KACE?
body: KACE is a centrally funded service that is available to all university departments. Each department can obtain a secure and containerized KACE organization to help support and maintain Rutgers-owned equipment. The administration and configuration of each feature provided by the K1000 appliance are unique to each organization. This provides each department with the ability to fully manage the implementation within their environment.

title: FAQ What data does KACE collect from a computer?
body:
The KACE agent collects available data via Microsoft’s Windows Management Instrumentation and the System Profiler on Mac systems. The data includes, but is not limited to:
•	System hardware (CPU, RAM, Hard Disks, etc.)
•	Make, model & serial/service tag information
•	Networking (IP Address, MAC address, etc.)
•	System software inventory
•	Operating system version and patch level
•	Software licenses & metering statistics (if enabled)
•	Historical records (changes in software, hardware, system name, etc.)

title: FAQ Who can access the data collected by KACE and where is the data stored?
body: All data collected by KACE is stored in a secure database within the KACE appliance. Data for each KACE organization is stored in its unique, secure database, accessible only by the administrator responsible for that organization. The aggregate data is accessible to authorized OIT KACE administrators. However, no changes to the systems are made without consent from the organization's admins. These administrators may produce periodic reports to OIT senior management during events such as a university-wide software audit.

title: FAQ Will KACE scan storage devices attached to my computer (USB drives and/or hard drives)?
body: The KACE agent scans the hard disk for capacity, utilization, and drive designations (for example, "C:\" or "D:\"). The agent does not collect any data on the contents of the disks, or file structure.

title: FAQ Will my system always be connected to the KACE appliance?
body: The KACE agent maintains a low resource connection to the KACE appliance for the entire time a system is powered on. This constant connection allows tasks to be sent on demand from the appliance to the client systems. If a system goes into sleep, hibernation, or is powered off, the connection to the appliance is severed. Once the client system exits these states, it will automatically reconnect to the appliance.

title: FAQ Will the KACE agent hinder the performance of my computer?
body: The KACE agent utilizes less than 2% of the system resources and runs as a background service. The client system will perform an inventory scan on a schedule and then upload the data to the KACE appliance. This scan is not intrusive and does not impede the end user's information or computer performance.

Overview
The LinkedIn Learning tools were developed by the Office of Information Technology. They are a set of simple shortcuts that help content creators share valid URLs and other useful information from LinkedIn Learning with users. 
The main focus of the tool is to be able to provide SSO URLs so that users can be properly authenticated through Rutgers Central Authentication for content at Rutgers.
Accessing the Tools
The tools are available at the University Software Portal.
Using the Tools
The tool is essentially a single form input that accepts either Lynda.com URLs, LinkedIn Learning URLs, or LinkedIn Learning URNs.
Although the form morphs depending on which tab is selected at the top, you can enter any type of valid input into the text area. You can even mix and match. Just separate each input by a carriage return (enter).
Sample inputs are provided within each tab. Clicking Try It will fill the text area with the sample value.
